questions.question: CNN vs ViT for a dataset with only 10K labeled images—how do you decide, and what changes with 10M images?
questions.say:
At 10K images the real question is not CNN versus ViT, it is whether you have a good pretrained model - and you almost always do, so fine-tune a pretrained ViT.

If you genuinely had to train from scratch on 10K images, the CNN wins clearly. Convolutions hand you locality, translation equivariance and weight sharing for free; a ViT has to learn all of that from data it does not have, so a ResNet-50 beats a from-scratch ViT-B comfortably. But a ViT pretrained on CLIP, DINOv2 or ImageNet-21K and then fine-tuned on your 10K will beat that ResNet, because at this data scale pretrained features dominate inductive bias.

At 10M the ViT catches up and passes, because its flexibility becomes an asset - it learns spatial structure suited to your task rather than the one convolutions assume. I would be careful about quoting a crossover number, though. The original ViT paper only brackets it somewhere between ImageNet-1K, about 1.3 million images, and ImageNet-21K, about 14 million, and it is heavily recipe-dependent: DeiT-style augmentation and distillation push it down toward a million or below. ConvNeXt also shows a modernised CNN largely matching ViT at scale, so the gap is not as clean as it is usually told.

Practically: CLIP ViT-B/16 fine-tuned is a strong default, EfficientNet or MobileNet if you are latency-bound on device, Swin or ConvNeXt if you need multi-scale features for detection or segmentation.
numbers: ImageNet-1K ~1.3M images, ImageNet-21K ~14M - the from-scratch crossover sits somewhere in between
red_flags: "ViT is better, it is newer" - data efficiency is the entire question at 10K.
Never considering a pretrained model, which is the practical answer.
Quoting a precise crossover threshold as though it were a known constant.
followups: What is ConvNeXt and why does it complicate this debate?
How do you handle ViT position embeddings at a new resolution?
Would you ever train a ViT from scratch on a small dataset?
questions.answer_source:
The core tradeoff is inductive bias vs.\ data-driven learning. CNNs have strong built-in biases (locality, translation equivariance, weight sharing) that make them data-efficient. ViTs have minimal inductive bias and rely on learning spatial structure from data, requiring much more data to match CNNs.

**With 10K labeled images:** CNN is the clear winner from scratch. A ResNet-50 trained on 10K images will significantly outperform a ViT-B trained from scratch because the ViT must learn what convolutions provide for free—local feature extraction, spatial hierarchy. However, a pre-trained ViT (from CLIP, DINOv2, or ImageNet-21K) fine-tuned on 10K images will likely beat a randomly initialized CNN. So the real question is: **do you have a good pre-trained model?** If yes, ViT wins due to superior pre-trained features. If training from scratch, CNN wins.

**With 10M images:** ViT catches up and surpasses CNN. At this scale, ViT's flexibility becomes an advantage—it learns task-specific spatial patterns that may be more optimal than CNN's hardcoded biases. ViT also tends to scale more gracefully with model size, though this advantage is not absolute—ConvNeXt shows a modernized CNN can largely match ViT at scale. The crossover point where a from-scratch ViT matches a CNN is not a single number: the original ViT paper's evidence only brackets it somewhere between ImageNet-1k scale ($\sim$1.3M images) and ImageNet-21k scale ($\sim$14M), and it is heavily recipe-dependent—DeiT-style augmentation and distillation push it down toward $\sim$1M images or below. Quote the bracket and the recipe-dependence, not a false-precision threshold.

**Practical recommendation:** Almost always use a pre-trained model. CLIP ViT-B/16 fine-tuned on 10K domain-specific images is a strong default. If latency is critical (mobile/edge), use EfficientNet or MobileNet. If you need multi-scale features (detection, segmentation), use Swin Transformer or ConvNeXt.
questions.red_flags_source:
- "ViT is always better because it's newer"—data efficiency matters
 
- Ignoring the option of pre-trained models (the most practical choice)
 
- Not knowing that ViTs struggle with small datasets when trained from scratch
questions.followups_source: "What is ConvNeXt and why does it matter for this debate?" "How do you handle ViT position embeddings at different resolutions?" "Would you ever train a ViT from scratch on a small dataset?"

questions.question: Explain how DETR works and why it represents a paradigm shift in object detection.
questions.say:
DETR turns detection into direct set prediction: the model emits a fixed set of a hundred predictions in one shot, and training matches them one-to-one against ground truth with the Hungarian algorithm. That matching is the real innovation — because each ground-truth object can be claimed by exactly one prediction, duplicates are penalized by construction, and anchors and non-max suppression drop out of the pipeline entirely.

Mechanically: a CNN backbone produces a feature map, a transformer encoder does global self-attention over it, and a decoder takes a hundred learned object queries and cross-attends to the encoder output. Each query comes out as a class plus a box, with a no-object class for the empty slots. The queries aren't image patches — they're learned slots that specialize by region and object scale.

Why it's a shift: the whole detector is differentiable end to end, with no anchor design and no hand-tuned IoU thresholds, and it extends to panoptic segmentation by adding a mask head.

The limitations are real, though. Original DETR needed 500 epochs to converge because attention starts diffuse, against roughly 12 to 36 for Faster R-CNN, and it was weak on small objects. Deformable DETR fixed most of that by attending to a few learned sample points instead of every position, cutting training to about 50 epochs, and DINO-DETR added denoising and contrastive queries to reach state of the art.
red_flags: Not mentioning bipartite matching — it is the innovation
Claiming DETR strictly beats Faster R-CNN
Confusing object queries with image patch tokens
followups: What are object queries, mechanistically?
How does Deformable DETR fix the convergence problem?
How would you adapt this for video?
questions.answer_source:
DETR (Detection Transformer, Carion et al., ECCV 2020) reimagines object detection as a direct **set prediction** problem, eliminating all hand-crafted components from the detection pipeline.

**Architecture.** (1) A CNN backbone (ResNet-50) extracts a feature map from the input image. (2) A Transformer encoder processes the flattened feature map with self-attention, allowing global reasoning across the entire image. (3) A Transformer decoder receives $N$ learnable "object queries" (typically $N = 100$) and produces $N$ predictions via cross-attention to the encoder output. Each query specializes in detecting certain object types, sizes, or spatial regions. (4) Each prediction is a tuple (class, bounding box), with class "no object" for empty slots.

**Training: bipartite matching.** The key innovation is using the Hungarian algorithm to find the optimal one-to-one assignment between predictions and ground truth objects. The matching cost combines classification loss and box regression loss (L1 + GIoU). This eliminates the need for anchor boxes and NMS entirely—the set loss naturally prevents duplicate detections.

**Why it's a paradigm shift.** (1) **End-to-end**: No anchor design, no NMS, no hand-tuned IoU thresholds. The entire detection pipeline is differentiable. (2) **Global reasoning**: Self-attention enables reasoning about object relationships (e.g., "this region is already claimed by another query"). (3) **Simplicity**: The code is dramatically simpler than Faster R-CNN. (4) **Extensibility**: Trivially extends to panoptic segmentation by adding a mask head.

**Limitations.** (1) Slow training: 500 epochs (vs.\ 12–36 for Faster R-CNN) because attention is initially diffuse. (2) Weak on small objects: global attention dilutes focus on small regions. (3) Fixed number of queries limits max detections per image.

**Improvements.** Deformable DETR uses deformable attention (attend to learned sparse points instead of all positions), reducing training to 50 epochs and improving small-object detection. DINO-DETR adds denoising training and contrastive queries, achieving SOTA.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Not mentioning bipartite matching—it's DETR's most important innovation
 
- Saying "DETR is always better than Faster R-CNN"—it has real limitations
 
- Confusing object queries with image patch tokens
questions.followups_source: "What are object queries, mechanistically?" "How does Deformable DETR fix the training speed problem?" "How would you adapt DETR for video object detection?"

questions.question: Explain the reparameterization trick and why it's needed for VAE training. What happens without it?
questions.say:
It's what makes the encoder trainable at all — without it there's no gradient path back through the sampling step.

The problem: the encoder outputs a mean and a standard deviation, you draw z from that Gaussian, you hand z to the decoder. But "draw a random number" has no derivative with respect to the mu and sigma that produced it, so there's nothing to send back to the encoder. The decoder trains fine; the encoder is stranded.

The trick is to move the randomness outside the parameters. Instead of sampling z from a normal with mean mu and variance sigma squared, you sample epsilon from a standard normal and set z equal to mu plus sigma times epsilon. Identical distribution, but now z is a deterministic, differentiable function of mu and sigma, with epsilon just an input. The derivative with respect to mu is one, with respect to sigma is epsilon, and the chain rule works normally.

Without it you're not completely stuck — you can use the score-function estimator, REINFORCE, and it's unbiased. But the variance is brutal, high enough that VAE training is impractical. So this isn't mathematical elegance, it's a low-variance estimator that lets you train with ordinary SGD.

The limitation worth volunteering: it only works when your distribution is a deterministic transform of a fixed base distribution. Gaussians, yes. Discrete latents, no — which is exactly why VQ-VAE uses a straight-through estimator and why Gumbel-Softmax exists.
red_flags: "It's a mathematical convenience" — training genuinely fails without it.
Not identifying that the core problem is backpropagating through a sampling operation.
Claiming there is no alternative — REINFORCE works, it's just far too high-variance.
followups: How does VQ-VAE handle the non-differentiable codebook lookup?
What is the Gumbel-Softmax trick?
Can you reparameterize a non-Gaussian posterior?
questions.answer_source:
The reparameterization trick solves a fundamental problem: how to backpropagate through a stochastic sampling operation.

**The problem.** In a VAE, the encoder outputs parameters $\mu$ and $\sigma$ of a Gaussian distribution $q_\phi(z|x) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_\phi(x), \sigma_\phi^2(x))$. We need to sample $z \sim q_\phi(z|x)$ to pass to the decoder, then compute the ELBO loss and backpropagate. But sampling is a non-differentiable operation—there's no gradient of "draw a random number" with respect to $\mu$ and $\sigma$. Without gradients, we can't train the encoder with standard backpropagation.

**The solution.** Instead of sampling $z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ directly, reparameterize as a deterministic function of the parameters plus external randomness:
$$z = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \epsilon, \quad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$$
Now $z$ is a deterministic, differentiable function of $\mu$ and $\sigma$ (with fixed $\epsilon$). Gradients flow through $\mu$ and $\sigma$ via the chain rule: $\partial z / \partial \mu = I$ and $\partial z / \partial \sigma = \epsilon$. The stochasticity comes from $\epsilon$, which is independent of the parameters.

**Why it matters.** Without the reparameterization trick, we'd need to use high-variance REINFORCE-style gradient estimators (score function estimator): $\nabla_\phi \E_q[f(z)] = \E_q[f(z) \nabla_\phi \log q_\phi(z|x)]$. This works in theory but has extremely high variance, making training impractical. The reparameterization trick provides a low-variance gradient estimator that enables stable VAE training with standard SGD.

**Limitations.** Only works for distributions that can be expressed as deterministic transforms of a fixed base distribution. Works for Gaussians, but not directly for discrete distributions (which is why VQ-VAE uses a different approach with straight-through estimators).
questions.red_flags_source:
- "It's just a mathematical convenience"—it's essential, training fails without it
 
- Not knowing that the core issue is backpropagating through sampling
 
- Confusing reparameterization with other variance reduction techniques
questions.followups_source: "How does VQ-VAE handle the non-differentiability of discrete codebook lookup?" "What is the Gumbel-Softmax trick?" "Can you apply reparameterization to non-Gaussian distributions?"

questions.question: Diffusion models vs GANs vs VAEs vs autoregressive models—give me a comparison table and decision framework for different generation tasks.
questions.answer_source:
Each generative model family has distinct strengths, and the right choice depends on the application constraints.

**Quality.** Diffusion models produce the highest quality images (lowest FID on ImageNet). GANs are close but suffer from mode collapse. VAEs produce blurrier outputs due to the MSE reconstruction + KL regularization tradeoff. Autoregressive models (PixelCNN, image GPT) produce good quality but are extremely slow for images.

**Diversity.** Diffusion models have the best mode coverage (no mode collapse by design—the forward process destroys modes uniformly). GANs are prone to mode collapse (generator ignores parts of the data distribution). VAEs have good coverage but smooth over fine details. Autoregressive models have good diversity.

**Sampling speed.** GANs are fastest: single forward pass ($\sim$10ms). VAEs are fast: encode + decode ($\sim$10ms). Autoregressive: slow, scales linearly with output size ($\sim$minutes for images). Diffusion: slow, requires 20–1000 denoising steps ($\sim$1–30 seconds). DDIM and consistency models reduce diffusion steps to 1–4 with quality tradeoff.

**Training stability.** VAEs: stable (straightforward ELBO optimization). Diffusion: stable (simple MSE denoising loss). Autoregressive: stable (cross-entropy). GANs: notoriously unstable (minimax game, mode collapse, vanishing gradients). WGAN-GP helps but doesn't fully solve instability.

**Controllability.** Diffusion models: excellent (classifier-free guidance, ControlNet, IP-Adapter). GANs: style control via StyleGAN's W-space, conditional generation. VAEs: smooth latent space enables interpolation. Autoregressive: conditioning via prompts.

**Decision framework:**

 
- Text-to-image, maximum quality $\to$ Diffusion (Stable Diffusion, DALL-E 3)
 
- Real-time generation ($<$50ms) $\to$ GAN (StyleGAN) or distilled diffusion
 
- Representation learning, smooth latent $\to$ VAE
 
- Likelihood estimation needed $\to$ VAE or autoregressive
 
- Language generation $\to$ Autoregressive (GPT-style)
 
- Training simplicity, no tuning $\to$ Diffusion or VAE
questions.red_flags_source:
- "Diffusion is always best"—GANs are still unbeatable for single-step generation
 
- Not knowing that GANs suffer from mode collapse
 
- Ignoring sampling speed as a critical production constraint
questions.followups_source: "What are consistency models and how do they relate to diffusion?" "When would you still choose a GAN in 2025?" "How does VQ-VAE + autoregressive (DALL-E 1) compare to latent diffusion (DALL-E 2/3)?"
questions.say:
There isn't really a table, there are three axes — sample quality, sampling cost, and training stability — and each family sits at a different corner.

Diffusion gives the best image quality and the best mode coverage, with no mode collapse by construction, and it trains stably on a plain denoising loss. What you pay is sampling: 20 to 1000 network evaluations, so seconds rather than milliseconds, though DDIM, distillation and consistency models pull that down to one to four steps with some quality cost. GANs are the mirror image — one forward pass, about ten milliseconds, but a minimax objective that's notoriously unstable and prone to mode collapse, where the generator quietly drops parts of the distribution. VAEs train stably, sample fast, give you a likelihood bound and a smooth latent space you can interpolate in, but reconstruct blurrily because of the MSE-plus-KL tradeoff. Autoregressive models are stable, give exact likelihoods, and own language outright; for images they're slow if you generate pixel by pixel, which is why modern image AR models generate discrete tokens from a VQ tokenizer instead.

My decision rule: text-to-image at maximum quality is diffusion. Real-time generation is a GAN or a distilled diffusion model. Anything where you need a likelihood is VAE or autoregressive. Smooth latent space for representation work is a VAE. Language is autoregressive. And controllability matters more than people expect — classifier-free guidance, ControlNet and IP-Adapter are a large part of why diffusion won image generation in production.
numbers: GAN sampling: single forward pass, ~10 ms
Diffusion sampling: 20–1000 steps; distilled/consistency variants get to 1–4
red_flags: "Diffusion is always best" — single-step generation still belongs to GANs or distilled diffusion.
Not knowing what mode collapse is or that GANs suffer from it.
Ignoring sampling cost, which is usually the binding production constraint.
followups: What are consistency models and how do they relate to diffusion?
When would you still pick a GAN today?
How does VQ-VAE plus autoregressive compare to latent diffusion?
questions.notes: Corrected a stale framing in the source: it characterized autoregressive image models as pixel-by-pixel (PixelCNN, image GPT) and therefore "extremely slow." Modern image AR models generate discrete tokens from a VQ tokenizer, which the source itself acknowledges in its follow-up about VQ-VAE. Also softened the source's red flag that GANs are "unbeatable for single-step generation" — distilled and consistency diffusion models now compete there, which the same source concedes elsewhere.

questions.question: What is classifier-free guidance and why does it improve generation quality in diffusion models?
questions.answer_source:
Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a technique that improves the quality and condition-adherence of conditional diffusion models by amplifying the effect of the conditioning signal during sampling.

**Mechanism.** During training, the model learns both conditional and unconditional denoising: randomly drop the conditioning (text prompt) with probability $p$ (typically 10–20\
$$\tilde{\epsilon}_\theta(x_t, c) = \epsilon_\theta(x_t, \emptyset) + w \cdot (\epsilon_\theta(x_t, c) - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, \emptyset))$$
where $w$ is the guidance scale (typically 5–15). The term $(\epsilon_\theta(x_t, c) - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, \emptyset))$ is the "direction" that the conditioning pushes the prediction. Multiplying by $w > 1$ amplifies this direction.

**Intuition.** Think of it as implicit classifier guidance. Ho & Salimans (2022) showed that the CFG update is equivalent to using an implicit classifier $p(c|x_t) \propto p(x_t|c)/p(x_t)$. The guidance scale $w$ controls how strongly the model follows this implicit classifier. Higher $w$ means stronger conditioning adherence—images match the prompt more closely but lose diversity.

**Why it works.** Without guidance ($w = 1$), diffusion models produce diverse but sometimes off-topic samples. The conditional distribution $p(x|c)$ is broad. CFG sharpens this distribution, producing samples closer to the mode of $p(x|c)$. This trades diversity for quality and relevance—exactly the tradeoff users want for text-to-image generation.

**Guidance scale tradeoff.** $w = 1$: no guidance (pure conditional sampling). $w = 3$–$7$: balanced quality and diversity. $w = 7$–$15$: strong prompt adherence, reduced diversity. $w > 20$: oversaturation, artifacts, loss of coherence. Stable Diffusion defaults to $w = 7.5$.

**Why not classifier guidance?** Earlier work (Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021) used a separately trained classifier to guide diffusion. CFG is superior because: (1) no extra classifier needed, (2) works with any conditioning (text, image, class label), (3) the conditioning comes from the same model, ensuring coherence.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Confusing classifier-free guidance with classifier guidance
 
- Not knowing that it requires training with random conditioning dropout
 
- Saying "higher guidance is always better"—there's a quality-diversity tradeoff

questions.say:
Classifier-free guidance amplifies the conditioning at sampling time by extrapolating away from the unconditional prediction. During training you randomly drop the text condition, typically ten to twenty percent of the time, so the same network learns both conditional and unconditional denoising. At sampling you run it both ways and take the unconditional prediction plus w times the difference between the two. That difference is the direction the prompt is pushing; scaling it above one pushes further than the model would go on its own.

Why it helps: the conditional distribution the model learned is broad, so plain conditional sampling gives diverse but often off-prompt images, and guidance sharpens toward the modes. Ho and Salimans showed the update is equivalent to guiding with an implicit classifier built from the ratio of conditional to unconditional density, which is why you don't need to train a separate one - and that's the difference from classifier guidance, which did.

It's a knob, not free quality. Three to seven is balanced, seven to fifteen gives strong adherence with less diversity, Stable Diffusion defaults to 7.5, and past twenty you get oversaturation and artifacts. So CFG trades diversity for prompt adherence, which for text-to-image happens to be the trade users want.
numbers: Condition dropout during training: ~10-20%
Guidance scale: 3-7 balanced, 7-15 strong adherence, Stable Diffusion default 7.5
red_flags: Confuses it with classifier guidance, which needs a separately trained noisy-image classifier.
Doesn't know it requires condition dropout during training; it isn't a pure inference-time trick.
"Higher guidance is always better" - past the sweet spot you get oversaturation and lose diversity.

questions.question: Explain the ELBO derivation for VAEs and why the model produces blurry images. What fixes exist?
questions.say:
The ELBO exists because the marginal likelihood is intractable - you would have to integrate the decoder over every possible latent. So you introduce an approximate posterior q of z given x, and then log p of x splits exactly into two pieces: the ELBO, and the KL between your approximate posterior and the true one. That second piece is non-negative, which is precisely why the first is a lower bound. Maximising the ELBO does three things at once: improves reconstruction, pulls the posterior toward the prior, and tightens the bound.

The blurriness has two causes and people usually name only one. With a Gaussian decoder the reconstruction term is just negative squared error, and when several outputs are plausible for one latent, the MSE-optimal prediction is their mean - and an average of sharp images is a blurry image. On top of that, the KL term squeezes the posterior toward a standard normal, compressing the latent space and stripping capacity that fine detail would need.

The fixes attack one or the other. Perceptual loss swaps pixel MSE for a distance in VGG feature space. VAE-GAN adds a discriminator that penalises blur directly. VQ-VAE replaces the continuous Gaussian latent with a discrete codebook and is the one that really solved this. Hierarchical VAEs like NVAE stack latents at several scales. And you can simply down-weight the KL term - a beta below one, which is the opposite of the setting beta-VAE was originally proposed for.
red_flags: Reciting the ELBO without saying where it comes from or why it is a bound.
Blaming blurriness only on the KL term - the MSE reconstruction is at least as responsible.
Not knowing VQ-VAE as the main answer to blurriness.
followups: What is posterior collapse and how would you detect it?
How does the VQ-VAE codebook actually get trained?
What does the size of the ELBO gap tell you?
questions.whiteboard: $$\log p_\theta(x) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z|x)}[\log p_\theta(x|z)] - \mathrm{KL}\!\left(q_\phi(z|x)\,\|\,p(z)\right)}_{\text{ELBO}} + \mathrm{KL}\!\left(q_\phi(z|x)\,\|\,p_\theta(z|x)\right)$$ Say while writing: this is an identity, not an approximation. Point at the last term, say it is a KL so it is non-negative, and that single fact is the whole reason the bracket is a lower bound.
questions.notes: Flagged a source slip: the source lists "beta-VAE: reduce the KL weight (beta < 1)" as a fix. beta-VAE as published uses beta > 1 for disentanglement; down-weighting the KL for sharper reconstructions is the opposite setting. Said so explicitly in `say` rather than propagating it.
questions.answer_source:
The ELBO (Evidence Lower Bound) arises from the fact that the marginal likelihood $\log p_\theta(x) = \log \int p_\theta(x|z) p(z) dz$ is intractable (the integral has no closed form). We introduce an approximate posterior $q_\phi(z|x)$ and derive:

$\log p_\theta(x) = \underbrace{\E_{q_\phi(z|x)}[\log p_\theta(x|z)] - \KL(q_\phi(z|x) \| p(z))}_{\text{ELBO}} + \underbrace{\KL(q_\phi(z|x) \| p_\theta(z|x))}_{\geq 0}$

Since the last KL term is non-negative, the ELBO is a lower bound on $\log p(x)$. Maximizing the ELBO simultaneously: (1) maximizes the reconstruction quality (first term), (2) keeps the approximate posterior close to the prior (second term), and (3) tightens the bound (reduces the gap KL term).

**Why blurriness.** The reconstruction term $\E_{q(z|x)}[\log p(x|z)]$ with a Gaussian decoder and MSE loss computes $-\|x - \hat{x}\|^2$. When the model is uncertain (multiple valid outputs for a given $z$), MSE-optimal prediction is the **mean** of all valid outputs—which is inherently blurry. Additionally, the KL term forces $q(z|x)$ toward $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$, compressing the latent space and reducing the model's ability to represent fine details. The combination means VAEs hedge their bets, producing the average of possible outputs rather than a sharp specific sample.

**Fixes:** (1) **Perceptual loss**: Replace MSE with a loss computed on VGG features, which penalizes structural differences rather than pixel differences. (2) **VAE-GAN**: Add a discriminator that penalizes blurriness directly. (3) **VQ-VAE**: Replace continuous latent with a discrete codebook, eliminating the Gaussian bottleneck. The straight-through estimator handles non-differentiability. (4) **Hierarchical VAE** (NVAE): Multiple levels of latent variables, with each level capturing different scales of detail. (5) **$\beta$-VAE**: Reduce the KL weight ($\beta < 1$) to prioritize reconstruction over regularization, at the cost of less regular latent space.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Stating the ELBO without deriving it or explaining where it comes from
 
- Blaming blurriness solely on the KL term—MSE reconstruction is equally responsible
 
- Not knowing about VQ-VAE as the primary solution to blurriness
questions.followups_source: "What is posterior collapse and how do you detect it?" "How does VQ-VAE's codebook learning work?" "What's the relationship between the ELBO gap and the quality of the approximate posterior?"

questions.question: How does Stable Diffusion work end-to-end? Walk through the architecture from text prompt to generated image.
questions.say:
Stable Diffusion is a latent diffusion model — the expensive denoising happens in a compressed latent space instead of in pixels, and that single decision is what made it runnable on consumer GPUs. A pretrained VAE compresses a 512-by-512 image into a 64-by-64-by-4 latent, about 48 times fewer numbers, so each denoising step costs roughly 64 times less and the attention layers become affordable, since attention is quadratic in the number of positions.

End to end: CLIP's text encoder turns the prompt into a sequence of embeddings. You sample pure Gaussian noise at the latent shape. Then a U-Net of roughly 860 million parameters iteratively predicts and removes noise. It's conditioned two ways — the timestep enters through an embedding, and the text enters through cross-attention layers where latent positions attend to the prompt tokens. That cross-attention is the conditioning mechanism; if someone asks how the prompt actually influences the image, that's the answer.

At every step you run the U-Net twice, once with the prompt and once with an empty prompt, then push the prediction away from the unconditional one. That's classifier-free guidance, typically around a scale of 7.5, and it's why generation costs two forward passes per step rather than one. After 20 to 50 steps with DDIM or a similar sampler, the VAE decoder turns the clean latent back into pixels.
numbers: 512×512×3 → 64×64×4 latent: ~48× fewer values
U-Net ~860M params; CFG scale ~7.5; 20–50 sampling steps
CFG costs 2 U-Net passes per step
red_flags: Saying the diffusion runs in pixel space
Not naming cross-attention as the text conditioning path
Forgetting that classifier-free guidance doubles compute per step
followups: What changed in SDXL relative to SD 1.5?
What is ControlNet doing architecturally?
How would you fine-tune this for one art style?
questions.answer_source:
Stable Diffusion is a latent diffusion model that performs the expensive denoising process in a compressed latent space rather than pixel space.

**Architecture components:** (1) **Text encoder** (CLIP ViT-L/14): Converts the text prompt into a sequence of embedding vectors ($77 \times 768$ for SD 1.5). These embeddings capture the semantic content of the prompt. (2) **VAE encoder/decoder**: Pre-trained autoencoder that compresses images $512 \times 512 \times 3 \to 64 \times 64 \times 4$ (8$\times$ spatial compression). The latent space preserves perceptual quality while being 48$\times$ smaller. (3) **U-Net denoiser** ($\sim$860M params): The core model that iteratively removes noise from the latent. Contains ResNet blocks, self-attention layers, and cross-attention layers (where text conditioning is injected). Conditioned on both the text embedding (via cross-attention) and the timestep $t$ (via sinusoidal embedding + adaptive layer norm).

**Inference pipeline:** (1) Encode text prompt to embeddings via CLIP. (2) Sample random noise in latent space: $z_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ at shape $64 \times 64 \times 4$. (3) Iteratively denoise using the U-Net. At each step $t$, compute two noise predictions: $\epsilon_\theta(z_t, c)$ (conditional, with text) and $\epsilon_\theta(z_t, \emptyset)$ (unconditional, null text). (4) Apply classifier-free guidance: $\tilde{\epsilon} = \epsilon_\emptyset + w(\epsilon_c - \epsilon_\emptyset)$ with $w = 7.5$. (5) Update $z_t \to z_{t-1}$ using the DDPM or DDIM update rule. (6) After all steps (typically 20–50), decode the clean latent $z_0$ to pixel space: $x = \text{Decoder}(z_0)$ producing a $512 \times 512$ image.

**Why latent space?** Running diffusion in pixel space at $512 \times 512$ would require the U-Net to process $262\text{K}$ spatial positions per step—impractical. In latent space at $64 \times 64$, only $4\text{K}$ positions, which is $\sim$64$\times$ fewer operations and enables attention layers (which are $O(n^2)$).

**Fine-tuning methods:** LoRA (low-rank adaptation on U-Net attention layers) for style transfer, DreamBooth (few-shot personalization), textual inversion (learn new text embeddings for concepts), ControlNet (add spatial conditioning like edges, depth, pose).
questions.red_flags_source:
- Saying diffusion happens in pixel space—it's in latent space
 
- Not mentioning cross-attention as the conditioning mechanism
 
- Forgetting that CFG requires two forward passes per step

questions.question: How do you handle the cold start problem for new users and new items?
questions.say:
Cold start is a data problem, not a model problem — the job is to design the system so it collects useful signal fast, and new users and new items need different answers.

For new users, you fall back on what you know without interactions: popularity, plus content and context features — device, locale, referral source, whatever the signup flow gives you. Ask a couple of preference questions at onboarding if the product tolerates it. Then run a bandit — Thompson sampling or epsilon-greedy — so the first handful of interactions actually move the profile instead of re-serving the same popularity list.

For new items, place the item in embedding space from its content: run title, description and image through encoders, or give it a content-derived semantic ID so it inherits signal from similar items that already have history. Then buy the interaction data deliberately — a small forced-impression budget — and log the propensities, so what you collect is usable for training rather than one more biased sample.

The Staff-level addition is where in the funnel this happens. Cold items have to be handled at retrieval, not just reranking: if the candidate generator never surfaces the item, nothing downstream rescues it. And cold start ends at different scales — a handful of interactions gives you a usable user profile, but you need hundreds of impressions before item statistics are stable.
red_flags: "Just use collaborative filtering" — there is no interaction data, that's the premise.
No exploration story, so the system never collects the signal it's missing.
Fixing it only in the ranker — a cold item retrieval never surfaces can't be rescued downstream.
followups: How do you balance exploration against user experience?
How would you evaluate whether the cold-start strategy is working?
How much forced-impression budget is enough?
questions.answer_source:
Cold start is a **data** problem, not a model problem—the system should be designed to collect useful signal quickly, and users and items need different strategies.

**New users**: start from popularity and content/context features (demographics, device, referral source), ask preferences at onboarding, and use bandits (Thompson sampling, epsilon-greedy) to learn from the first interactions quickly.

**New items**: place the item in embedding space via its content (text/image encoders, or a content-derived semantic ID so it inherits signal from similar items), and buy interaction data with deliberate exploration—a small forced-impression budget, propensity-logged so the resulting data is usable without bias.

**The Staff-level addition**: cold items must be handled at the **retrieval** stage, not just re-ranking—an item the candidate generator never surfaces cannot be rescued downstream—and cold start "ends" at different scales (a handful of interactions for a user profile, hundreds of impressions for stable item statistics).

- No mention of exploration or of where in the funnel cold items get their chance

questions.question: Two-tower vs. interaction-based models for candidate generation—when would you use each?
questions.answer_source:
The choice is dictated by the computational budget of the pipeline stage, not by model preference.

**Two-tower** encodes user and item independently; the only interaction is the final dot product. That restriction is what enables retrieval: item embeddings are pre-computed into an ANN index, online cost is one user-tower pass plus a lookup, independent of corpus size. **Interaction-based** models (DLRM, DCN, DIN) compute joint user-item representations—cross features, attention over behavior history—and are far more expressive, but the score cannot be pre-computed, so every candidate costs a forward pass.

**Decision**: retrieval over millions of items $\rightarrow$ two-tower (nothing else is sub-linear in corpus size); ranking over hundreds $\rightarrow$ interaction-based. The gap between them is bridged operationally (a pre-ranking stage with a distilled model) and at training time (hard negatives and distillation from the ranker into the two-tower).
questions.red_flags_source:
- "Use the more accurate model everywhere" (ignores that retrieval cost must not scale with corpus size)
 
- Conflating retrieval and ranking constraints
questions.followups_source: "Can you make two-tower more expressive without losing pre-computation?" "What ANN index would you use and why?"
questions.say:
The computational budget of the pipeline stage decides it, not which model is more accurate. Two-tower encodes user and item independently and the only interaction is a dot product at the very end. That restriction is precisely what makes retrieval possible: item embeddings are precomputed into an ANN index offline, so online you run one user-tower pass and a lookup, and the cost is independent of corpus size. Interaction-based models — DLRM, DCN, DIN — compute a joint user-item representation with cross features and attention over behavior history. They're far more expressive, but the score depends on the pair, so nothing is precomputable and every candidate costs a forward pass.

So: retrieval over millions of items is two-tower, because nothing else is sub-linear in corpus size. Ranking a few hundred candidates is interaction-based, because you can afford it there and the expressiveness is what actually moves the metric.

The interesting part is how you close the gap. Operationally, you put a pre-ranking stage with a distilled model between the two. At training time, you mine hard negatives and distill the ranker's scores into the two-tower, so the retrieval model inherits some of what the ranker knows without giving up precomputation.
red_flags: "Use the more accurate model everywhere" — ignores that retrieval cost must not scale with corpus size.
Conflating retrieval and ranking constraints as if they were the same problem.
No mention of how the two stages are bridged (distillation, hard negatives, pre-ranking).

questions.question: INT8 vs INT4 vs FP8 quantization—what is your decision framework?
questions.answer_source:
The choice depends on three factors: target hardware, acceptable accuracy loss, and whether you are quantizing for inference or training.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Quantization format decision matrix}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{lXXX}
\toprule
**Property** & **INT8** & **INT4** & **FP8 (E4M3)** 
\midrule
Memory reduction & $2\times$ (vs.\ FP16) & $4\times$ (vs.\ FP16) & $2\times$ (vs.\ FP16) 
Accuracy loss & Near-zero ($<$0.5\
Hardware support & Broad (A100, V100, CPU) & Limited (needs dequant kernels) & H100+ only 
Calibration effort & Minimal (SmoothQuant) & Moderate (GPTQ/AWQ, hours) & Minimal (per-tensor scaling) 
Best method & SmoothQuant, W8A8 & GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF & Native FP8 (torch.float8) 
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

**INT8** is the default for inference. SmoothQuant enables both weight and activation quantization (W8A8) by migrating quantization difficulty from activations (which have outlier channels) to weights (which are easier to quantize). Near-zero accuracy loss on most models. Use it on any hardware that supports INT8 tensor cores.

**INT4** is for memory-constrained deployment. GPTQ uses approximate second-order information (Hessian) to quantize weights layer-by-layer, adjusting remaining weights to compensate for quantization error. AWQ is faster—it identifies and protects the $\sim$1\

**FP8** is the new default for H100+ inference (and increasingly training). E4M3 format (4 exponent, 3 mantissa bits) provides better dynamic range than INT8 for the same 8-bit budget. Per-tensor dynamic scaling handles outliers without the need for SmoothQuant-style preprocessing. Native hardware support means minimal kernel engineering.

**Decision framework:**

 
- H100+ hardware $\to$ FP8 (E4M3) by default—simplest and fastest
 
- A100/older GPU $\to$ INT8 (SmoothQuant) by default
 
- Need to fit a larger model on fewer GPUs $\to$ INT4 (AWQ or GPTQ)
 
- CPU inference (llama.cpp) $\to$ GGUF with mixed precision (important layers at Q5/Q6, others at Q4)
 
- Training $\to$ FP8 on H100+ for $\sim$$2\times$ throughput; otherwise BF16
questions.red_flags_source:
- "INT4 is always better because it uses less memory"—INT4 has meaningful accuracy degradation, especially on reasoning tasks. The right precision depends on your accuracy budget.
 
- "FP8 and INT8 are the same thing in different formats"—FP8 has floating-point dynamic range (can represent very small and very large values); INT8 has fixed range determined by the scale/zero-point. FP8 handles activation outliers more naturally.
 
- "Quantization doesn't affect model quality"—it does, especially at INT4 and below. Always benchmark on your specific task, not just perplexity.
questions.followups_source: "How does SmoothQuant handle activation outliers?" "Why does INT4 degrade math and code more than general text?" "Can you combine INT4 weights with INT8 activations?" "What is the GGUF format and why does it matter for CPU inference?"
questions.say:
I choose on hardware first, then accuracy budget. On Hopper and newer, FP8 in E4M3 is the default: native tensor-core support, per-tensor dynamic scaling, half the memory of FP16, near-zero quality loss, almost no kernel engineering. FP8 beats INT8 at the same bit width because of dynamic range - floating point absorbs activation outliers, where INT8's fixed scale and zero point get stretched by them.

On A100-class or older hardware, or on CPU, INT8 is the answer, and the technique is SmoothQuant. It migrates quantization difficulty out of activations, which have nasty outlier channels, into weights, which are well behaved, and that's what makes W8A8 work at all. Expect under half a percent perplexity change.

INT4 is for when you must fit a bigger model on fewer GPUs and you'll pay for it. GPTQ quantizes layer by layer using approximate second-order information, compensating with the weights it hasn't done yet; AWQ is faster and protects the roughly one percent of weight channels that see large activations. Both give usable models, but degradation lands on reasoning, math and code rather than general text, so benchmark on your task, not perplexity.

Two places this has moved: FP8 is no longer H100-only, since Ada-generation cards have it too, and Blackwell adds native FP4, which makes four-bit a first-class hardware path.
numbers: INT8: <0.5% perplexity loss; INT4: ~1-3%
AWQ protects the ~1% of weight channels with the largest activations
red_flags: "INT4 always, it uses least memory" - the degradation lands on reasoning and code, and it needs a stated accuracy budget.
"FP8 and INT8 are the same eight bits" - FP8 has floating-point dynamic range, which is the whole point for activations.
Validates only on perplexity instead of the task the model actually does.
followups: How does SmoothQuant move difficulty from activations into weights?
Why does INT4 hurt math and code more than general text?
Can you combine INT4 weights with INT8 activations?
questions.notes: Corrected a stale claim: the source says FP8 is "H100+ only." Ada-generation GPUs (L4/L40S, RTX 40-series) also have FP8 tensor cores, and Blackwell adds native FP4, which changes the INT4 calculus the source frames as needing dequant kernels. Both added in one closing sentence.

questions.question: Your model's loss plateaus after initial descent. Walk through your debugging process.
questions.say:
I work down a fixed list, most common cause first, and the first thing I check is the learning rate.

A plateau very often just means the LR has decayed too far to escape the current basin. So I look at the schedule - step decay that dropped too hard is the classic - and I probe by multiplying the current LR by three to ten, or switching to cosine with warm restarts.

Next I split train from validation. Both plateaued and high means underfitting, so add capacity. Training low and validation flat means overfitting, so regularisation or more data. Both flat at a reasonable value may just mean I am near the noise floor for this data quality.

Then per-layer gradient norms. If the early layers sit at 1e-6 while the late layers are at 1e-2, gradients are vanishing and the early layers are effectively frozen; that points at residuals, pre-norm versus post-norm, or initialisation.

Then the data pipeline, which is the step people skip. Is the loader actually shuffling? Is label noise capping what is achievable? The clean test is to try to overfit a single batch to near-zero loss - if the model can, then the model and the loss are correct and it is an optimisation or data-scale problem. After that I would double width or depth purely as a diagnostic, and if it really is a sharp minimum, try a larger batch, SWA, or SAM.
red_flags: "I would just train longer" - plateaus rarely resolve without changing something.
Swapping the architecture before diagnosing the root cause.
Never auditing the data pipeline or trying to overfit a single batch.
followups: How do you tell underfitting from a data-quality ceiling?
What if raising the learning rate makes it diverge?
How does batch size change the loss landscape?
questions.answer_source:
I follow a structured diagnostic hierarchy, ordered from most common to least common cause:

 
- **Learning rate schedule.** Is the LR already too small? A plateau often means the current LR cannot escape the current basin. I check the schedule—if using step decay, the LR may have dropped too aggressively. I try cosine annealing with warm restarts, or simply multiply the current LR by 3–10$\times$ as a probe.

 
- **Train vs.\ validation loss.** If both are plateaued and high, the model is underfitting—I increase capacity (wider or deeper). If training loss is low but validation is plateaued, the model is overfitting and I need regularization or more data. If both plateau at a reasonable level, I may be near the Bayes-optimal error for this data quality.

 
- **Gradient norms per layer.** I log $\|\nabla_\theta \loss\|$ per layer. If early layers show norms $10^{-6}$ while later layers show $10^{-2}$, vanishing gradients are freezing the early layers. Fix: add residual connections, switch to pre-norm, or check initialization.

 
- **Data pipeline audit.** Is the data loader repeating batches or not shuffling properly? Are there label noise issues capping achievable loss? I check by training on a small subset—if the model can overfit a single batch to near-zero loss, the model and loss are correct and the issue is optimization or data scale.

 
- **Model capacity.** Double the width or depth as a diagnostic. If loss improves, the original model was too small.

 
- **Loss landscape.** The model may be stuck in a sharp local minimum. I try increasing batch size (smoother gradients), SWA (averages across minima), or SAM (penalizes sharpness explicitly).
questions.red_flags_source:
- "I would just train longer"—plateaus rarely resolve by training longer without changing something.
 
- "I would try a different architecture"—this is premature without diagnosing the root cause first.
questions.followups_source: "How do you distinguish underfitting from a data quality ceiling?" "What if increasing LR causes divergence?" "How does batch size affect the loss landscape?"

questions.question: Adam vs SGD with momentum—when would you pick each?
questions.say:
Adam for anything transformer-shaped, SGD with momentum where you have a known vision recipe and generalization is the whole game. The mechanical reason is gradient-scale heterogeneity: in a transformer the embeddings, the attention projections and the layer norms sit at very different gradient magnitudes, and one global step size can't serve all of them. Adam's per-parameter normalization handles that for free, which is why nobody trains an LLM with plain SGD.

SGD with momentum still holds up on well-studied convnet tasks with a tuned cosine schedule. The uniform step size acts as implicit regularization — the extra gradient noise helps you settle in flatter minima — and if you have the tuning budget and a recipe someone already validated, it's hard to beat. I'd also reach for Adam for fast prototyping, for GANs, and anywhere extensive learning-rate tuning isn't realistic.

The nuance I'd volunteer is that the gap has largely closed, and the old "SGD generalizes better" folklore mostly came from comparing SGD against Adam with plain L2 rather than decoupled weight decay. In Adam, L2 added into the gradient gets divided by the same running second-moment estimate, so it's attenuated exactly on the parameters with the largest gradients and you end up under-regularized without noticing. AdamW decouples the decay from the adaptive step and mostly erases the difference — ConvNeXt is the clean example of a modern convnet trained that way.
red_flags: "Adam always, it converges faster" — ignores the generalization story on vision
"SGD is obsolete"
Not distinguishing L2 in the loss from decoupled weight decay in Adam
followups: Why might Adam generalize worse?
How do adaptive learning rates relate to sharp minima?
How does weight decay interact differently with each optimizer?
questions.answer_source:
**SGD with momentum** when: Training a CNN on a well-studied task (ImageNet, detection) with a known recipe, and generalization matters most. SGD with a tuned cosine schedule consistently finds flatter minima on vision tasks. The uniform step size across parameters acts as implicit regularization—the gradient noise from non-adaptive updates helps escape sharp minima.

**Adam(W)** when: Training Transformers, LLMs, or any model with highly heterogeneous gradient scales across parameters. Attention layers have Q/K/V projections, embeddings, and layer norms all at different gradient magnitudes—Adam's per-parameter adaptive rate handles this naturally. Also preferred for: fast prototyping (less LR sensitivity), GANs (unstable landscapes), and any setting where extensive LR tuning is infeasible.

**The nuanced point:** The gap has narrowed. AdamW with proper decoupled weight decay and cosine schedule now matches SGD on many vision benchmarks (see ConvNeXt). The older "SGD generalizes better" result was mostly comparing SGD against Adam **without** decoupled weight decay—the L2 regularization gets attenuated by Adam's adaptive scaling, leading to effectively under-regularized models.
questions.red_flags_source:
- "Adam is always better because it converges faster"—ignores the generalization gap on vision tasks and the importance of the loss landscape geometry.
 
- "SGD is obsolete"—SGD remains the gold standard in well-tuned vision pipelines and has theoretical advantages for generalization.
 
- Confusing L2 regularization with decoupled weight decay in the context of Adam.

questions.question: Training loss is NaN after 1000 steps. Walk through your debugging process.
questions.say:
NaN means an Inf or an invalid operation got into the graph, and the fact that it's 1000 steps in already tells me something: a bad epsilon or corrupt data usually fires at step one, so I'd start with what grows.

First move is to look at gradient norms in the steps before the NaN. If they're climbing — 1e2, then 1e5, then 1e12, then NaN — it's exploding gradients, and the fix is clipping at 1.0, warmup, and probably a lower learning rate. If gradient norms are flat and then it's suddenly NaN, that's a different animal: a single bad op or a single bad batch.

Then in order of how often it's actually the cause. Check FP16 overflow — FP16 tops out around 65,500, and anything past that is Inf and then NaN on the next op; switching to BF16 and watching the problem vanish is a one-experiment diagnosis. Check log of zero and divide by zero: use the framework's fused cross-entropy rather than hand-rolling log-softmax, and make sure every normalization has its epsilon. Assert on the input batch, because corrupt data happens — just less often than people assume.

If none of that isolates it, register forward hooks and find the first module that emits a NaN. That's mechanical and always works; I don't start there because the gradient-norm trajectory usually answers it in two minutes.
numbers: FP16 max ~65,504; BF16 range ~3.4e38 (same exponent as FP32)
red_flags: "Set the LR to 1e-6 and hope" — that's guessing, and a low enough LR hides the bug while making training useless.
Assuming data first; exploding gradients and numerical instability are more common in practice.
Never looking at the gradient-norm trajectory before the NaN, which is where the diagnosis actually lives.
followups: What if it only NaNs in mixed precision and never in FP32?
How do you debug a NaN that only some ranks see in distributed training?
What's the difference in root cause between NaN and Inf?
questions.answer_source:
NaN loss means a numerical infinity or invalid value has propagated through the computation graph. I debug systematically from most common to least common cause:

**Step 1 — Check gradients before the NaN.** Insert `torch.autograd.detect_anomaly()` or log gradient norms every step. If gradient norms are growing exponentially in the steps before the NaN (e.g., $10^2 \to 10^5 \to 10^{12} \to \text{NaN}$), the cause is exploding gradients. **Fix:** Add gradient norm clipping with $c = 1.0$; reduce learning rate.

**Step 2 — Check data for NaN/Inf.** Add assertions on input batches: `assert not torch.isnan(x).any()`. Corrupted data (missing values, encoding errors) can inject NaN at the source. **Fix:** Clean the data pipeline; add input validation.

**Step 3 — Check for numerically unstable operations.** Common culprits:

 
- $\log(0)$ — if a softmax output reaches exactly 0 and you compute cross-entropy as $-\log(p)$. **Fix:** Use `F.cross_entropy` (numerically stable log-softmax), or add $\epsilon = 10^{-8}$ inside the log.
 
- Division by zero — LayerNorm with zero variance, or custom normalization. **Fix:** Ensure $\epsilon$ is present in denominators.
 
- $\exp(\text{large value})$ overflow — in attention logits or loss computation. **Fix:** Subtract the max before exponentiation (log-sum-exp trick).

**Step 4 — Check FP16 overflow.** FP16 overflows at $\sim 65{,}504$. If activations or gradients exceed this, they become Inf, then NaN on the next operation. **Experiment:** Switch to BF16 (range $\sim 3.4 \times 10^{38}$) or FP32 and see if the NaN disappears. **Fix:** Use BF16; tune the dynamic loss scaler; or identify which layer produces large activations.

**Step 5 — Check learning rate.** A learning rate that is too high causes parameter values to blow up. **Experiment:** Reduce LR by $10\times$. If training stabilizes, the original LR was too high for this architecture. **Fix:** Add warmup (especially critical for Transformers); reduce LR; ensure weight initialization is appropriate.

**Step 6 — Binary search for the guilty layer.** If the above steps do not isolate the cause, register forward hooks on each layer to check for NaN outputs. Run training until the NaN appears and find the first layer to produce it.
questions.red_flags_source:
- "Set LR to $10^{-6}$ and hope it works"—this is not debugging, it is guessing. A very low LR may mask the problem while making training useless.
 
- "NaN is usually a data problem"—while data can cause NaN, numerical instability and exploding gradients are more common in practice.

questions.question: Your 70B pretraining run diverges at 200B tokens. Give a full differential diagnosis, ordered by prior probability, with the cheapest discriminating experiment for each.
questions.answer_source:
Context first: 200B tokens deep means the code has been correct for weeks—so "bug in the model" has low prior, and anything that changed **at** 200B tokens has high prior. My differential, ordered by prior probability for a mature stack, each with the cheapest experiment that discriminates it:

 
- \textbf{Data–optimizer-state interaction (the PaLM-style spike, prior $\sim$40\

 
- \textbf{Logit growth / attention entropy collapse (prior $\sim$20\

 
- \textbf{Data distribution boundary (prior $\sim$15\

 
- \textbf{Hardware / silent data corruption (prior $\sim$10\

 
- \textbf{Numerics / precision (prior $\sim$10\

 
- \textbf{Software change / schedule cliff (prior $\sim$5\

The meta-answer: order by prior $\times$ cost-to-test, run the treatment for the most probable cause (rewind + skip) concurrently with the free log-reading diagnostics, and only then spend compute on replay experiments. Preserve the diverged checkpoint and the exact data cursor—every discriminator above depends on deterministic replay.
questions.red_flags_source:
- "Restart from scratch with a lower LR"—throws away 200B tokens of compute to treat an undiagnosed disease, and lowers final quality if the real cause was a bad node.
 
- "Find and delete the bad documents"—the PaLM skip-batch result shows spikes are state–data interactions; the same data replayed from a different state is usually fine. Filtering is not the primary fix.
 
- No mention of reading existing logs before spending cluster-hours on experiments.
questions.followups_source: "What monitoring would have caught this 5,000 steps earlier?" "When would you accept adding QK-norm mid-run?" "How do you make a 16K-GPU run bitwise-replayable, and what does determinism cost?"
questions.say:
Context first: 200 billion tokens in, the code has been correct for weeks — so "bug in the model" has a low prior, and anything that changed at 200B has a high one.

Most likely, call it forty percent, is a data-optimizer-state interaction — the PaLM-style spike, where a window of batches interacts badly with the current optimizer state. The cheapest discriminator is also the fix: rewind a few hundred steps and skip 200 to 500 batches over the window. If it sails through, diagnosis confirmed for a few cluster-hours, and I'd start that immediately, in parallel with everything below.

Around twenty percent is logit growth or attention entropy collapse, and that one is free — read the logs. Max attention logits and z-loss should show a slow ramp over thousands of steps, not a step change. Fifteen percent is a data boundary that changed by design: curriculum switch, new mixture, new shard, sequence-length extension — one grep of the schedule against the token count settles it. Ten percent is hardware or silent data corruption: replay the same steps from the same checkpoint on a different node set, and if it doesn't reproduce, quarantine those nodes. Ten percent numerics — replay the window in higher precision. Five percent a software change or a botched optimizer-state restore on resume, which an audit of the run log will show.

The meta-answer is order by prior times cost-to-test, and preserve the diverged checkpoint and the exact data cursor, because every one of those discriminators needs deterministic replay.

questions.question: A node dies every 3 hours on your 16K-GPU run. Design the recovery system.
questions.answer_source:
First, establish that this failure rate is **expected**, not a broken cluster: 16{,}384 GPUs at $\sim$50K-hour per-GPU MTBF gives $\approx 0.33$ failures/hour—one every 3 hours is exactly the Llama-3 405B experience (419 unexpected interruptions in 54 days on 16K H100s). So the design goal is not "stop failures" but "make each failure cost minutes, automatically." I would budget the system around four components:

**1. Checkpoint cadence—do the math.** Cluster MTBF $M = 3$ h $= 10{,}800$ s. With a naive synchronous checkpoint costing $\delta = 60$ s of stalled training, the Young/Daly optimum is $\tau \approx \sqrt{2\delta M} = \sqrt{2 \times 60 \times 10{,}800} \approx 19$ min. Expected waste per failure $\approx \tau/2 \approx 9.5$ min of lost work, plus $\sim$5\

**2. Make checkpoints nearly free.** Two standard steps: (a) **sharded** checkpoints—each rank writes its own parameter/optimizer shard (ZeRO/FSDP already hold state sharded), so write bandwidth scales with the cluster; (b) **asynchronous** checkpoints—snapshot to host memory in seconds, resume training, persist to durable storage in the background. That drives the training-visible $\delta$ to seconds, which by the same formula justifies checkpointing every few minutes; per-failure loss drops to a couple of minutes of work. The end state is torchft-style in-memory recovery: checkpoint replicas live in peer host/GPU memory across DP replica groups, and a failed group restores from a live peer with no storage round-trip, while the other groups continue.

**3. Automate detect–quarantine–replace with hot spares.** Recovery latency is dominated by detection and re-provisioning, so: health watchdogs (NCCL timeout tuned down from the default, heartbeats, ECC/Xid monitors) detect within seconds; the scheduler drains and quarantines the node; a **hot spare**—warm, image-loaded, network-configured; I would reserve $\sim$1–2\

**4. Handle the failures that don't kill the job.** Two classes are nastier than clean deaths: **stragglers**—a throttling GPU makes every synchronous step slow; detect via per-rank step-time and collective-wait profiling, evict ranks consistently last into the all-reduce—and **silent data corruption**: NaN/Inf watchdogs on loss and grad norms with automatic rewind, periodic redundant recomputation to catch a GPU computing wrong values, and a replay-on-different-hardware protocol before blaming the optimizer (ties into the loss-spike playbook).

**Sanity check the budget:** 8 failures/day $\times$ ($\sim$2 min lost work + $\sim$3 min restore) $\approx$ 40 GPU-cluster-minutes/day $\approx$ 3\
questions.red_flags_source:
- "Checkpoint every hour" (or any cadence not derived from MTBF and checkpoint cost)—the interviewer is testing exactly this arithmetic.
 
- Treating the failure rate as abnormal ("first, fix the hardware")—at 16K GPUs this rate **is** healthy hardware.
 
- No automation story: a design where a human notices the failure has already lost the game—at one failure per 3 hours, on-call humans are the bottleneck and the error source.
 
- Ignoring stragglers and SDC—the failures that don't throw errors cost more than the ones that do.

questions.say:
One failure every three hours at 16K GPUs is healthy hardware, not a broken cluster. Sixteen thousand GPUs at roughly a 50,000-hour per-GPU MTBF is about a third of a failure per hour - exactly the Llama-3 405B experience, 419 unexpected interruptions in 54 days. So the goal isn't fewer failures, it's making each one cost minutes with nobody paged.

I'd derive the checkpoint cadence, not guess it. Three-hour MTBF against a sixty-second synchronous checkpoint gives a Young-Daly optimum near nineteen minutes, so about ten minutes of lost work per failure. But the square root says the real lever is shrinking that sixty seconds: sharded writes, each rank persisting its own shard since FSDP already holds state that way, plus async checkpointing - snapshot to host memory, resume, flush in the background. Visible cost drops to seconds, so you checkpoint every few minutes. The end state is in-memory replicas across data-parallel groups, restoring from a live peer with no storage round trip.

Then automate detect, quarantine, replace. NCCL timeouts tuned down, heartbeats and ECC monitors catching it in seconds, the scheduler draining the node, and a hot spare - one or two percent of the fleet kept warm - spliced in. Node death to training resumed in single-digit minutes, no human.

And budget for the failures that don't crash: stragglers, caught by per-rank step-time profiling, and silent data corruption, caught by NaN watchdogs and periodic redundant recompute. Those cost more than the clean deaths.

Llama-3 405B: 419 unexpected interruptions in 54 days on 16K H100s

questions.question: How much GPU memory do you need to fine-tune a 13B parameter model with LoRA versus full fine-tuning?
questions.say:
Full fine-tuning a 13B model runs about 240 to 270 gigabytes, LoRA gets you to roughly 60 to 85, and QLoRA to under 40. The gap is not about parameter count, it is about what the optimiser has to hold.

Full fine-tuning in BF16 mixed precision with AdamW is 26 gigs of BF16 weights, 52 of FP32 master weights, 104 of momentum and variance, and 26 of gradients. That is 208 before activations, which at batch four, sequence 2048 and forty layers add another 30 to 60 with checkpointing. Four A100-80s with FSDP or ZeRO-3, minimum.

With LoRA at rank 16 on the Q and V projections you are training about 13 million parameters, roughly a tenth of a percent. The base model is frozen, so it costs 26 gigs of BF16 weights and nothing else: no master copy, no optimiser state, no gradients for it. The adapter's own weights, gradients and optimiser state together are under a quarter of a gig. Activations are essentially unchanged, because you still run the full forward pass. Total: one A100-80.

QLoRA quantises the frozen base to four-bit, so 6.5 gigs instead of 26, landing around 37 total - a single 40-gigabyte A100 or a 48-gigabyte workstation card.

The thing to say out loud is that the saving comes from the frozen base needing no optimiser state. The small parameter count on its own would only be worth about 0.2 gigabytes.
numbers: Full FT 13B: 26 + 52 + 104 + 26 = ~208 GB before activations
LoRA r=16 on Q/V of 40 layers: ~13M trainable params, ~0.1% of the model
QLoRA: INT4 base 6.5 GB, ~37 GB total
red_flags: "LoRA is cheaper because it has fewer parameters" - true but not the mechanism; the frozen base carrying no optimiser state is.
Forgetting activation memory, which is roughly the same for LoRA and full fine-tuning.
Not knowing AdamW holds master weights plus two moments per trainable parameter.
followups: What LoRA rank would you start at for 13B?
When is full fine-tuning worth the extra hardware?
How does LoRA interact with quantisation at inference time?
questions.notes: Corrected a stale hardware claim: the source calls 48 GB a "consumer GPU". Consumer cards top out at 24-32 GB; 48 GB is a workstation part, so `say` calls it that.
questions.answer_source:
**Full fine-tuning (BF16 mixed precision with AdamW):**

Per-parameter costs:

 
- BF16 parameters: $13\text{B} \times 2 = 26$ GB
 
- FP32 master weights: $13\text{B} \times 4 = 52$ GB
 
- FP32 optimizer states ($m$ + $v$): $13\text{B} \times 8 = 104$ GB
 
- BF16 gradients: $13\text{B} \times 2 = 26$ GB
 
- **Subtotal (parameters):** $\sim$208 GB

Activation memory depends on batch size and sequence length. For a typical setup ($b=4$, $s=2048$, $d=5120$, 40 layers): roughly 30–60 GB with gradient checkpointing. **Total: $\sim$240–270 GB.** This requires at minimum 4$\times$ A100-80GB with FSDP/ZeRO-3.

**LoRA fine-tuning (rank $r = 16$, adapting Q/V projections):**

Trainable parameters: Each adapted layer adds $2 \times d \times r = 2 \times 5120 \times 16 = 163{,}840$ parameters. With $\sim$80 adapted weight matrices (Q and V in 40 layers), total trainable params $\approx 80 \times 163{,}840 \approx 13\text{M}$ (0.1\

 
- Base model (frozen, BF16): $13\text{B} \times 2 = 26$ GB (no gradients, no optimizer states)
 
- LoRA parameters (BF16): $13\text{M} \times 2 \approx 0.03$ GB
 
- LoRA optimizer states (FP32 $m$ + $v$): $13\text{M} \times 8 \approx 0.10$ GB
 
- LoRA gradients (BF16): $13\text{M} \times 2 \approx 0.03$ GB
 
- **Subtotal (parameters):** $\sim$26.2 GB

Activation memory is similar (you still run forward through all layers), so $\sim$30–60 GB with checkpointing. **Total: $\sim$56–86 GB.** This fits on a **single** A100-80GB.

**QLoRA (4-bit quantized base + LoRA):**

Base model in INT4: $13\text{B} \times 0.5 = 6.5$ GB. Plus LoRA overhead ($\sim$0.2 GB) plus activations ($\sim$30 GB with checkpointing). **Total: $\sim$37 GB.** Fits on a single A100-40GB or even a consumer GPU with 48 GB VRAM.

- "LoRA uses less memory because it has fewer parameters"—this is true but incomplete. The dominant saving is that the frozen base model needs **no gradients, no optimizer states, and no master weights**. The parameter count reduction alone would only save $\sim$0.2 GB.
 
- Forgetting activation memory—it is often the second-largest component and is nearly the same for LoRA and full fine-tuning.

questions.question: Data parallelism, tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism — what's your decision framework?
questions.say:
Three questions decide it: does the model fit on one GPU, what's the interconnect, and how many GPUs are there. Data parallelism is always the first choice — each rank takes different data and you all-reduce gradients once per step, so communication is one pass over the parameters and, with ring all-reduce, it doesn't grow with GPU count. If the model doesn't fit, shard optimizer state, gradients and parameters with FSDP or ZeRO before reaching for anything more exotic. That scales to hundreds of GPUs, bounded more by the critical batch size than by the network.

Tensor parallelism splits individual weight matrices, which means all-reducing activations inside every forward and backward pass, several times per layer. That only works over NVLink, 600-plus gigabytes a second inside a node. Running tensor parallel across nodes on InfiniBand at a tenth of that will destroy throughput, and it's the single most common bad answer to this question. So: tensor parallel within a node, degree four or eight, never across.

Pipeline parallelism splits layers across devices and only sends activations at stage boundaries, point to point, which is cheap enough to cross nodes. Its cost is the bubble — stages idle while the pipeline fills and drains — which you shrink with more micro-batches and interleaved 1F1B scheduling.

So: fits on one GPU, DDP. Fits in a node with sharding, FSDP. Larger, 3D — tensor within node, pipeline across nodes, data parallel over the replicas.
numbers: NVLink 600+ GB/s versus InfiniBand ~50 GB/s — why TP stays in-node
TP degree 4–8; past that, communication dominates
Pipeline bubble ≈ (P−1)/(M+P−1)
red_flags: Proposing tensor parallelism across nodes
Treating FSDP/ZeRO-3 and model parallelism as the same thing
No mention of the pipeline bubble or how to shrink it
followups: How do you choose TP/PP/DP degrees for a given cluster?
How do you minimize the pipeline bubble?
How does FSDP differ from ZeRO-3 in practice?
questions.answer_source:
The choice depends on three factors: **model size** (does it fit on one GPU?), **interconnect bandwidth** (NVLink vs.\ InfiniBand vs.\ Ethernet), and **number of GPUs**.

**Data Parallelism (DDP / FSDP / ZeRO):**

 
- **What it splits:** Data across GPUs. Each GPU processes different batches; gradients are synchronized.
 
- **Communication:** All-reduce of gradients once per step. Volume = $O(P)$ bytes, independent of GPU count (ring all-reduce).
 
- **When:** Model fits on one GPU (DDP), or fits with sharded optimizer/gradients (FSDP/ZeRO). **Always the first choice**—simplest and most efficient.
 
- **Scales to:** Hundreds of GPUs, limited by batch size (diminishing returns beyond critical batch size) and all-reduce latency.

**Tensor Parallelism (TP):**

 
- **What it splits:** Individual weight matrices across GPUs ($\mW$ split column-wise or row-wise).
 
- **Communication:** All-reduce of activations **within every forward and backward pass** (multiple times per layer). Very communication-intensive.
 
- **When:** A single layer is too large for one GPU, or you need to reduce per-GPU memory for large models. **Requires NVLink** (600+ GB/s)—never use across nodes on InfiniBand ($\sim$50 GB/s).
 
- **Scales to:** 4–8 GPUs within a single node. Beyond 8, the communication overhead dominates.

**Pipeline Parallelism (PP):**

 
- **What it splits:** Layers across GPUs (GPU 0 gets layers 1–20, GPU 1 gets layers 21–40, etc.).
 
- **Communication:** Point-to-point activation transfer between stages—only at stage boundaries, so lower bandwidth requirement than TP.
 
- **When:** Model is too large for one node even with TP. PP works across nodes because inter-stage communication is point-to-point and relatively low-bandwidth.
 
- **Limitation:** Pipeline bubble—GPUs idle while waiting for micro-batches. Bubble fraction $\approx (P-1)/(M+P-1)$ where $M$ is micro-batches and $P$ is pipeline stages. Mitigate by increasing $M$ or using interleaved schedules (1F1B).

**Decision framework:**

 
- Model fits on 1 GPU $\to$ **DDP only**
 
- Model fits on 1 node (8 GPUs) with sharding $\to$ **FSDP/ZeRO + optional TP within node**
 
- Model needs multiple nodes $\to$ **TP within node + PP across nodes + DP across PP replicas** (3D parallelism)
 
- $>$100B parameters $\to$ Full 3D parallelism with expert-level tuning of TP/PP/DP degrees
questions.red_flags_source:
- "Use tensor parallelism across nodes"—TP requires NVLink bandwidth. Cross-node TP on InfiniBand is $10\times$ slower and will destroy throughput.
 
- Treating FSDP/ZeRO-3 and model parallelism as interchangeable—FSDP shards parameters but gathers them in full for each layer's computation. Model parallelism actually splits the computation itself.

questions.question: Estimate the number of trainable parameters for LoRA with rank 16 on a 7B model.
questions.say:
About 17 million trainable parameters — roughly a quarter of a percent of the model.

The arithmetic: a 7B like Llama-7B is 32 layers with hidden dimension 4096. Target the attention projections — Q, K, V, O — and each is 4096 by 4096. LoRA replaces the update to each with an A and a B, so at rank 16 that's 16 times 4096, twice, about 131 thousand parameters per matrix. Four matrices per layer, 32 layers: 32 times 4 times 131K is 16.8 million. Against a 6.7 billion parameter base that's 0.25 percent. In memory it's about 34 megabytes at FP16 — nothing.

If you also target the feed-forward projections, those aren't square; for Llama they're 4096 by 11008, so each LoRA pair is 16 times the sum of those, about 242 thousand. Three of them per layer over 32 layers adds roughly 23 million, so you land near 40 million total — still well under one percent.

The thing I'd flag is that the parameter count isn't where the memory saving actually comes from. What matters is that you're not holding Adam's two moment tensors for 7 billion parameters. Trainable-parameter count is the headline number; the optimizer state is the reason it fits on the GPU.
numbers: LoRA r=16, attention only, 7B: 32 layers x 4 matrices x 2 x 4096 x 16 ~= 16.8M (~0.25% of base)
Adding FFN (4096 x 11008) adds ~23M, for ~40M total — still under 1%
red_flags: Forgetting the factor of two — there is both an A and a B matrix.
Not knowing the shape of a 7B: 32 layers, hidden dimension 4096.
Quoting total parameters when asked for trainable ones.

With 4 target matrices per layer and 32 layers: $32 \times 4 \times 131{,}072 = 16{,}777{,}216 \approx 16.8M$ parameters. This is about 0.25\

questions.question: Your LoRA fine-tuned model performs well on your test set but catastrophically forgets general capabilities. How do you fix it?
questions.answer_source: LoRA is supposed to mitigate catastrophic forgetting by keeping base weights frozen, so if it is still happening, the issue is likely one of several causes. First, the LoRA rank may be too high or alpha too large, giving the adapter excessive capacity to override base model behavior—reduce rank from 64 to 8–16 and ensure $\alpha/r \leq 1$. Second, the learning rate may be too high—LoRA adapters should use 1e-4 to 3e-4, not the 1e-5 typical of full FT. Third, too many epochs on narrow domain data causes the adapters to overfit to that distribution—use early stopping based on a held-out set that includes both domain and general examples. Fourth, the training data itself may be too narrow—mix in a fraction (10–20\

- "LoRA cannot cause catastrophic forgetting because the base weights are frozen"—the adapter itself can learn to override base model behavior
 
- Suggesting full fine-tuning as the fix (this would make forgetting worse)
 
- Not mentioning evaluation on general benchmarks
questions.followups_source: "How do you quantify catastrophic forgetting?" "What if you need aggressive domain adaptation AND general capabilities?" "Can you combine multiple LoRA adapters?"
questions.say:
First I'd confirm the forgetting is real rather than a vibe from a handful of prompts — run general benchmarks like MMLU and HellaSwag before and after, alongside the domain eval. Assuming it's real, the frame is that LoRA reduces forgetting but doesn't prevent it: the base weights are frozen, but the adapter sits in the forward path and can absolutely learn to override base behavior.

Then four levers, roughly in that order. Adapter capacity: rank 64 is usually more than the task needs, so drop to 8 or 16 and keep alpha over rank at or below one, which scales the update down. Learning rate: LoRA wants 1e-4 to 3e-4, and if someone has pushed well past that it's doing surgery rather than adaptation. Training length: too many epochs on narrow data overfits the adapter to that distribution, so early-stop on a held-out set that contains general examples as well as domain ones — domain-only validation will never show you this. And the data mix: fold in ten to twenty percent general-purpose data so the adapter never sees a world made only of your domain.

What I'd actually put in place for production is the gate: a general-capability eval suite that runs beside the domain eval, with deployment blocked unless both pass. And I wouldn't reach for full fine-tuning as the fix — that makes forgetting worse, not better.
numbers: LoRA LR: 1e-4 to 3e-4 (vs ~1e-5 for full fine-tuning)
Reduce rank 64 → 8–16, keep α/r ≤ 1
Mix in 10–20% general-purpose data
