questions.question: Your fine-tuned model echoes the prompt before answering—why?
questions.answer_source: The most likely cause is **missing loss masking on prompt tokens**. If the training loop set `labels = input_ids` without masking the prompt span to the ignore index ($-100$), the model was trained to predict prompt tokens as well as response tokens—and since prompts often dominate token counts, most of the gradient signal taught it to generate user-turn text. The trained behavior is exactly the symptom: given a prompt, produce more prompt-shaped text (echo or paraphrase it), then answer, and often invent a fresh user turn afterward. Verification takes minutes: decode one collated batch from the actual training pipeline and print which positions carry loss (`labels != -100`); if prompt positions carry loss, that is the bug. Fix: a completion-only collator (TRL's `DataCollatorForCompletionOnlyLM`, Axolotl's `train_on_inputs: false`) and retrain—cheap, since LoRA SFT at typical scale is an hours-long single-GPU job. Two differentials to rule out before retraining. First, **template mismatch**: if serving renders a different chat template than training—or omits the generation prompt—the model may be **completing the user's turn** rather than starting the assistant's; check by rendering the exact inference-time token sequence and diffing it against a training example. Second, **base-model residue**: a non-instruct base checkpoint fine-tuned on only a few hundred examples can echo as leftover pretraining behavior (documents that restate questions); the fix there is more or better SFT data, not the mask. The discriminating test: a masking bug produces echoing even when you replay a literal training example through the training-time template offline; a template mismatch disappears under that replay.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Immediately blaming the base model or "not enough data" without inspecting a collated training batch
 
- Not knowing the labels/ignore-index mechanics at all
 
- Proposing to hide it—a system prompt telling the model not to echo, or string-stripping the echoed prompt in postprocessing (an acceptable stopgap, but it leaves the model wasting tokens and signals you cannot find the root cause)

questions.question: LoRA vs QLoRA vs full fine-tuning vs prompt tuning—give a complete decision framework.
questions.say:
Default to LoRA and move off it only for a specific reason. Four axes drive it: data volume, hardware, quality bar, and how you will serve it.

LoRA is the default because it covers the common case - one to a hundred thousand examples on a single GPU. It trains a tenth of a percent to one percent of the parameters, reaches ninety-five to ninety-nine percent of full fine-tuning quality on most tasks, and merges back into the base weights so inference costs nothing extra. The killer feature is multi-task serving: swap adapters instead of duplicating the base model per task.

Full fine-tuning is for north of a hundred thousand good examples, multi-GPU infrastructure, and a quality bar LoRA has measurably failed to clear. Memory is the gate - weights, gradients and optimiser state come to four to eight times the weights alone depending on precision, so even a 7B is a multi-GPU job. The risk is catastrophic forgetting if you do not regularise or mix in general data.

QLoRA is LoRA over a four-bit base, three to four times less memory, which is how you fine-tune a 70B on one card. Quality parity with 16-bit LoRA is configuration-dependent; the paper reports it with NF4, double quantisation and adapters on all linear layers. Benchmark it, do not assume it.

Prompt tuning trains under a hundredth of a percent. The gap closes with scale but stays real below about 10B, so it is lightweight customisation at extreme scale, not domain adaptation.
numbers: LoRA: trains 0.1-1% of parameters, reaches 95-99% of full-FT quality
QLoRA: 3-4x memory reduction; fine-tunes a 70B on a single 24-80 GB GPU
Prompt tuning: <0.01% of parameters, gap stays significant below ~10B
red_flags: "Always full fine-tune for best results" with no cost-quality reasoning.
Treating QLoRA as strictly better than LoRA - parity is configuration-dependent and has to be verified per task.
Never mentioning serving, where adapter swapping is often the deciding factor.
followups: What about adapter layers, DoRA, or IA3?
Does LoRA work for pretraining?
How do you pick rank and alpha once you have chosen LoRA?

Use when you have $>$100K high-quality examples, multi-GPU infrastructure, and need maximum quality—for example, a flagship production model that justifies the cost. Memory is the gate: a 7B model needs roughly 60\,GB in FP16 (and $\sim$120\,GB in FP32) for weights, gradients, and optimizer states, i.e.\ 4–8$\times$ the weights alone. questions.question: You've chosen LoRA to adapt a 7B instruction-tuned model to an internal support-and-policy domain: 20K curated examples, one 80 GB GPU, and the adapter will be served alongside the general assistant. Pick rank, alpha, and target modules, and defend the choices.
questions.say:
I'd start at rank 16, alpha 32, adapters on all the linear projections — Q, K, V, O plus the FFN up, gate and down — with a learning rate around 2e-4, and treat all three as things I move once I have a held-out curve, not as a recipe.

Rank is capacity. At rank 16 on a 7B, attention-only is about 17 million trainable parameters; adding the FFN matrices doubles that to 40 million, under one percent of the base. With 20 thousand examples this is domain adaptation, not new-capability acquisition — the model already speaks the language and knows the format, it needs our policies and vocabulary — so the low-rank assumption holds. I'd still sweep 8 to 64; if quality is flat across that range, rank was never the binding constraint and I keep the smallest — small adapters are cheaper to store and swap.

Alpha isn't a second capacity knob. The adapter contributes alpha-over-r times BA, so only the ratio matters, and raising alpha at fixed rank is close to raising the learning rate on the adapter path — so I hold the ratio at two and tune the LR. One trap: vanilla LoRA divides by r rather than root r, so rank 64 with alpha fixed actually shrinks the update, and the bigger run looks flat for reasons unrelated to capacity. Above 64 I turn on rank-stabilized scaling.

And target modules move quality more than rank does — widening to the FFN beats raising r on attention alone.
numbers: r=16, all linear layers on a 7B: ~40M trainable params, ~0.6% of base
α/r = 2 as the working scale; tune LR, not both
LoRA LR ~2e-4 versus ~1e-5 for a full fine-tune

Treating α as capacity rather than the α/r scale on the update
"Use the highest rank you can afford" — ignores overfitting at 20K examples and per-adapter serving cost
followups: You went from rank 16 to 64 and nothing improved — what are the two explanations?
What changes with 500 examples instead of 20K?
What changes if the base model is 4-bit quantized?
questions.answer_source:
I would start at $r = 16$, $\alpha = 32$, adapters on all linear projections ($\mW_q, \mW_k, \mW_v, \mW_o$ plus the FFN up/gate/down matrices), learning rate 2e-4, and treat all three as things I will move once I have a held-out curve—not as a recipe.

**Rank is capacity, and capacity cuts both ways.** $r$ sets the dimension of the subspace the update can live in. The count $L \times M \times 2 \times d \times r$ (Section~) gives 16.8M trainable parameters for the four attention projections at $L = 32$, $d = 4096$, $r = 16$; adding the wider FFN matrices roughly doubles that to $\sim$40M, about 0.6\

**$\alpha$ is not a second capacity knob—it is the scale on the update.** The adapter contributes $\frac{\alpha}{r}\mB\mA\vx$, so only the **ratio** matters: $\alpha = r$ gives unit scale, $\alpha = 2r$ the common $2\times$ default. The practical consequence is that $\alpha$ and the learning rate are entangled—raising $\alpha$ at fixed $r$ is close to raising the effective LR on the adapter path—so I fix $\alpha/r$ and tune the learning rate, rather than tuning both. I would hold $\alpha/r = 2$ while chasing domain quality, and pull it toward $\alpha/r \le 1$ if general-capability evals start to slide, since the effective scale is the most direct lever on how hard the adapter overrides the frozen base. One rank-dependent trap: because vanilla LoRA divides by $r$ rather than $\sqrt{r}$, raising rank while holding $\alpha$ fixed **shrinks** the effective update, so a naive $r = 64$ run can look no better than $r = 16$ for reasons that have nothing to do with capacity. If I go above $r \approx 64$ I enable rank-stabilized scaling ($\alpha/\sqrt{r}$) so the added capacity is actually usable.

**Target modules move quality more than rank does.** Attention-only ($\mW_q, \mW_v$) is the cheapest configuration and a fine baseline, but the modern default is all linear layers including the FFN, which is where a good deal of factual and stylistic adaptation lives; the QLoRA ablations point the same way. Widening the target set is usually a better use of a fixed parameter budget than raising $r$ on a narrow set. If I also have to extend the tokenizer for domain vocabulary, the new embedding rows must be trainable alongside the adapter—LoRA on frozen embeddings cannot learn tokens the base has never seen.

**When I would raise rank.** Large distribution shift—a new language, a genuinely unfamiliar modality of text, or behavior the base model does not have at all—breaks the low-rank assumption, and the answer there is $r = 64$+ with all-linear targets and rank-stabilized scaling, or full fine-tuning if that still underperforms. That is not this task.

**How I would know I was wrong.** Train-loss plateau with validation still improving means underfitting: raise $r$ or widen targets. Validation improving while a general benchmark suite (MMLU, an instruction-following set, plus a held-out general chat slice) degrades means the adapter is overriding the base: lower $\alpha/r$, lower $r$, shorten training, or mix 10–20\

- Quotes a recipe ($r = 8$, $\alpha = 16$) with no reasoning about task difficulty, dataset size, or how it would be validated
 
- Treats $\alpha$ as an independent capacity knob rather than the scale $\alpha/r$ on the update
 
- "Just use the highest rank you can afford"—ignores overfitting and forgetting at 20K examples, and ignores per-adapter storage and serving cost
 
- Never mentions target-module choice, or assumes attention-only is the only option
 
- No empirical plan: no rank sweep, no general-capability eval to catch the override failure mode

questions.question: You fine-tuned a model and it performs well on your test set but poorly in production. What happened?
questions.say:
Nine times out of ten the test set simply isn't production, and I'd check that before anything else.

Distribution shift is hypothesis one. Curated test data is clean; production has typos, slang, truncated inputs, formats nobody anticipated, and users actively trying to break it. The check is cheap — pull a stratified sample of real production traffic, label a few hundred, and score the model on that. If the gap reproduces there, you've found it and you can stop.

Second, catastrophic forgetting. Aggressive fine-tuning overfits the model to a narrow slice and costs it the general capability it needs for everything outside that slice. Compare base against fine-tuned on a broad benchmark, not just your task. Fixes are lower learning rate, fewer epochs, LoRA rather than full fine-tuning, or mixing general-purpose data back into the fine-tuning mixture.

Third, leakage. If your test set overlaps the training data — near-duplicates, or just the same time window — the offline number was fiction. Split temporally and run near-duplicate detection across the two sets.

Fourth, metric mismatch. Accuracy or perplexity on clean inputs may just not correlate with what production cares about — task completion, escalation rate, user satisfaction. That one is the most common and the least often caught, because everyone's dashboard keeps saying the model is fine.

The durable fix for all four is the same: build the eval set out of production logs, and keep refreshing it.
red_flags: Jumping to "retrain on more data" before diagnosing which failure it is.
Not treating distribution shift as the first hypothesis.
Blaming model capacity with no evidence.
followups: How do you prevent catastrophic forgetting?
How do you build a test set that actually represents production?
What monitoring would have caught this earlier?
questions.answer_source: There are four primary failure modes to investigate in order. **1. Distribution shift**: The test set does not represent production traffic. Maybe the test data was curated and clean while production inputs include typos, slang, adversarial inputs, or edge cases the model never trained on. Fix: evaluate on production-like data before deploying, use stratified sampling from production logs. **2. Catastrophic forgetting**: Aggressive fine-tuning destroyed the model's general capabilities. The model overfits to the narrow fine-tuning distribution and cannot handle the broader range of production inputs. Fix: lower learning rate, fewer epochs, use LoRA instead of full fine-tuning, mix in general-purpose data during training. **3. Data leakage**: The test set overlaps with or is too similar to the training data, inflating offline metrics. Fix: strict temporal splits, near-duplicate detection between train and test, never evaluate on data from the same time window as training. **4. Evaluation metric mismatch**: The offline metric (e.g., perplexity, accuracy) does not correlate with the production success metric (e.g., user satisfaction, task completion rate). High accuracy on clean inputs says nothing about robustness on adversarial inputs. Fix: align offline evaluation to the actual business metric, add adversarial and edge-case test sets.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Jumping to "retrain with more data" without diagnosing the root cause
 
- Not considering distribution shift as the first hypothesis
 
- Blaming "the model isn't big enough" without evidence
questions.followups_source: "How do you prevent catastrophic forgetting?" "How do you build a test set that represents production?" "What monitoring would you put in place to catch this earlier?"

questions.question: What is TF-IDF? Derive the formula. When would you use it over neural embeddings?
questions.answer_source:
TF-IDF stands for Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency. It is a weighting scheme that
assigns higher scores to terms that are frequent in a specific document but rare across the
corpus.

**Term Frequency** measures how often a term $t$ appears in document $d$:
$\text{tf}(t, d) = f_{t,d}$. A sublinear variant uses $1 + \log f_{t,d}$ to dampen the
effect of very high counts.

**Inverse Document Frequency** measures how informative a term is:
$\text{idf}(t) = \log(N / \text{df}(t))$, where $N$ is the total number of documents and
$\text{df}(t)$ is the number of documents containing $t$. Common words like "the" appear
in nearly every document, so their IDF approaches zero. Rare, discriminative terms have high
IDF.

The combined score is $\text{tfidf}(t, d) = \text{tf}(t, d) \times \text{idf}(t)$.

I would use TF-IDF over neural embeddings when: (1) I need interpretable features—each
dimension corresponds to a specific term; (2) latency is critical—TF-IDF is a simple
sparse vector operation with no GPU needed; (3) training data is limited—TF-IDF requires
no labeled data, only corpus statistics; (4) the task relies on exact lexical matching, such
as keyword-based search or duplicate detection where semantics are not the bottleneck.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Saying "TF-IDF is outdated and should never be used."
 
- Not knowing the IDF formula or why the log is needed.
 
- Being unable to explain why common words get low scores.
 
- Forgetting to mention sublinear TF or document normalization.
questions.followups_source:
How does BM25 improve on TF-IDF? What is the vocabulary mismatch problem?
How would you combine TF-IDF with neural methods in a hybrid retrieval system?
questions.say:
TF-IDF scores a term high when it's frequent in this document and rare across the corpus. Term frequency is the count of the term in the document, usually dampened as one plus log count so a term appearing fifty times doesn't count fifty times as much as appearing once. Inverse document frequency is the log of total documents over documents containing that term. Multiply the two and that's the weight of that term in that document.

The log is doing real work. Document frequency spans orders of magnitude, so a raw ratio would let one rare term swamp everything; the log turns it into an additive weight on a sane scale. And the reason "the" scores near zero falls straight out — it appears in nearly every document, so N over df is about one and its log is about zero. You also normalize by document length, or long documents win by default.

I'd pick it over neural embeddings when I need interpretable features, because every dimension is a literal term; when latency matters and I don't want a GPU in the path; when there's no labeled data, since it needs only corpus statistics; or when the task is genuinely lexical — keyword search, duplicate detection, matching identifiers. In production I'd reach for BM25 over raw TF-IDF and run it beside a dense retriever, because the failure modes are complementary: lexical misses paraphrase, dense misses exact rare terms.
red_flags: "TF-IDF is outdated and should never be used" — it's still the right tool for lexical, low-latency, unlabeled settings.
Not knowing the IDF formula, or why the log is there.
Forgetting sublinear TF and document-length normalization.
followups: How does BM25 improve on TF-IDF?
What is the vocabulary mismatch problem?
How would you combine TF-IDF with neural retrieval in a hybrid system?

questions.question: Explain BM25. Why is it still used in production search systems?
questions.answer_source:
BM25 is a probabilistic retrieval function that scores the relevance of a document to a
query. It improves on TF-IDF in two key ways.

First, **term frequency saturation**: BM25 uses the formula $f(k_1+1)/(f+k_1)$ for
the TF component, which asymptotically approaches $k_1 + 1$ as term frequency $f$
increases. This means additional occurrences of a query term yield diminishing returns,
unlike raw TF which grows linearly.

Second, **document length normalization**: the denominator includes a factor
$k_1(1 - b + b \cdot |d|/d_{\text{avg}})$ that penalizes longer documents. A document
twice the average length needs roughly twice the term frequency to achieve the same score.
The parameter $b$ controls the strength of this normalization.

BM25 remains in production because it is: (1) **fast**—implemented via inverted
index lookup, handling millions of documents in milliseconds; (2) **requires no
training data**—only corpus statistics; (3) **robust**—works well across domains
without tuning; (4) **interpretable**—you can explain why a document ranked highly by
inspecting which query terms matched and their BM25 contributions; (5) **complementary
to neural methods**—modern hybrid systems use BM25 for exact lexical matching alongside
dense retrieval for semantic matching.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Not knowing the parameters $k_1$ and $b$ or their roles.
 
- Saying "BM25 is just TF-IDF" without explaining the differences.
 
- Not knowing that BM25 is still a production standard (Elasticsearch, Solr, Lucene).
questions.followups_source:
What are typical values for $k_1$ and $b$? How does BM25 handle multi-word
queries? What is BM25F? How would you combine BM25 with a dense retriever?
questions.say:
BM25 is a bag-of-words scoring function that fixes the two places raw TF-IDF is naive, and it's still the default lexical retriever in Lucene, Elasticsearch and Solr.

First is term-frequency saturation. In TF-IDF a document mentioning your query term twenty times scores twenty times one that mentions it once, which is obviously wrong. BM25 runs the count through a saturating function, controlled by k1, so the fifth occurrence adds far less than the second. Second is length normalization: the denominator scales with document length relative to the corpus average, controlled by b, so a document twice the average needs roughly twice the term frequency to score the same. That stops long documents winning by containing everything.

It survives because it's an inverted-index lookup, so milliseconds over hundreds of millions of documents; it needs no training data, just corpus statistics, so it works on day one in a new domain; and it's interpretable, so you can say exactly which query terms matched and what each contributed.

But the real reason is complementarity. Dense retrieval fails on exact matches - part numbers, rare proper nouns, code identifiers - which is precisely what lexical matching is good at, so every serious production system is hybrid.
numbers: Typical parameters: k1 around 1.2-2.0, b around 0.75
red_flags: "BM25 is just TF-IDF" without being able to name what changed.
Doesn't know what k1 and b control.
Treats it as legacy - it is the lexical half of essentially every production hybrid system.

questions.question: Explain the difference between rule-based, statistical, and neural NLP. When would you still use rule-based methods?
questions.say:
Three eras, and the difference is what gets learned versus what gets written by hand. Rule-based systems have humans writing the patterns - regexes, grammars, gazetteers. Statistical NLP learns the parameters from data but humans still engineer the features: HMMs, CRFs, n-gram models, TF-IDF. Neural NLP learns features and parameters together, end to end, from Word2Vec and LSTMs through BERT and GPT.

I would still reach for rules in about five situations, and I do regularly. When precision matters far more than recall and the target has a known format - dates, phone numbers, email addresses - a regex is exactly right and a model is the worse tool. When the domain is genuinely closed, like URL parsing or input validation. When a regulator or an auditor has to read the logic, which is common in content moderation. When speed is the constraint, since rule engines are orders of magnitude faster than any neural model. And when there is no training data at all and you have to encode domain knowledge directly.

What I would actually say about production systems is that the good ones are hybrids: rules on the front for normalisation and the obvious cases, a neural model in the middle, rules again on the back as guardrails and post-processing. Framing it as rules versus neural is the wrong frame - the question is which layer each belongs in.
red_flags: "Rule-based methods are obsolete" with no qualification.
Cannot give one concrete case where a regex beats a model.
Vague about what feature engineering meant in the statistical era.
followups: Give an example of a hybrid rule-plus-model system you would build.
How do you test and maintain a large rule set?
When does a rule system get too complex to keep?
questions.answer_source:
**Rule-based NLP** uses hand-crafted patterns: regular expressions, grammars,
gazetteers, and decision trees written by domain experts. It is interpretable and
deterministic but brittle, expensive to maintain, and fails to generalize.

**Statistical NLP** learns patterns from data using probabilistic models: HMMs for
sequence labeling, n-gram language models, CRFs, TF-IDF for retrieval. Features are
hand-engineered but model parameters are learned. This era achieved broad coverage but
required significant feature engineering expertise.

**Neural NLP** learns both features and parameters end-to-end from data. From
Word2Vec and LSTMs to BERT and GPT, neural methods progressively eliminated manual feature
engineering and achieved state-of-the-art on virtually every NLP benchmark.

I would still use rule-based methods when: (1) **Precision is critical and recall is
secondary**—e.g., extracting structured data from known formats (dates, phone numbers,
email addresses) where regex is 100\
closed}—e.g., parsing URLs, validating input formats, simple text normalization. (3)
**Interpretability is required by regulation**—e.g., content moderation rules that must
be auditable. (4) **Speed is paramount**—regex and rule engines are orders of
magnitude faster than neural models. (5) **No training data exists**—rules can be
written from domain knowledge alone.

In practice, the best production systems are hybrid: rule-based preprocessing and
post-processing with neural models in between.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Saying "rule-based methods are obsolete" without qualification.
 
- Not understanding the role of feature engineering in statistical NLP.
 
- Being unable to give a concrete scenario where rules are preferable.
questions.followups_source:
Give an example of a hybrid rule + ML system. How do you test and maintain
rules at scale? When does a rule-based system become too complex to maintain?

questions.question: Why use a CRF layer on top of BERT for NER instead of just a softmax classifier?
questions.say:
Because a softmax head makes each token's decision independently, and NER labels are a sequence with hard constraints between neighbours. BERT gives you rich input-side context — every token already sees the whole sentence — but nothing in a per-token softmax stops the model from emitting an impossible tag sequence like B-PER followed by I-ORG. Input-side dependency and output-side dependency are different things, and that distinction is really the whole answer.

A CRF adds a learned transition matrix over label pairs, scoring how compatible adjacent tags are, and then decodes the best-scoring whole sequence with Viterbi rather than taking an argmax at each position independently. It learns from data that I-PER can follow B-PER or I-PER but not B-ORG, and that an I- tag can't open an entity. You train it end to end with the encoder; the likelihood needs a partition function over all possible sequences, which the forward algorithm gives you in time linear in sequence length.

Where it earns its keep is low-data regimes, many entity types, and richer tag schemes like BIOES where there are more ways to be inconsistent. I'd also say the honest thing: with a large fine-tuned encoder and plenty of data the gain is often a few tenths of a point, and a constrained Viterbi decode with hand-written transition rules captures most of it without the extra training complexity.
red_flags: "BERT already models dependencies" without separating input-side from output-side
Not knowing what the transition matrix does or how the sequence is decoded
Claiming the CRF always helps — with a strong encoder and abundant data it's often marginal
followups: How is the CRF trained end to end with BERT?
What is the partition function and how is it computed?
What is label bias, and does a CRF suffer from it?
questions.notes: Source gave "O cannot directly follow an I- tag without a preceding B- tag" as an example of an invalid transition; that is wrong — O legitimately follows I-PER at the end of every entity. Replaced with correct examples (I-PER after B-ORG, an I- tag opening an entity).
questions.answer_source:
A softmax classifier on top of BERT makes **independent** predictions for
each token. At position $t$, it computes
$P(y_t \given \vx) = \softmax(\mW \vh_t + \vb)$, where $\vh_t$ is BERT's
contextualized representation. This means the prediction at position $t$
does not consider what labels were assigned to neighboring positions.

A CRF layer adds a transition score matrix $\mA \in \R^{K \times K}$ that
models the compatibility between adjacent labels. The probability of the
entire sequence becomes
$P(\vy \given \vx) \propto \exp(\sum_t h_t^{(y_t)} + \sum_t A_{y_{t-1}, y_t})$.

This captures output-side dependencies: the CRF learns that I-PER should
follow B-PER but not B-ORG, that O cannot directly follow an I- tag without a
preceding B- tag, and so on. Without the CRF, a softmax classifier might
produce invalid label sequences like "O I-PER I-ORG," which the CRF
transition matrix would prevent.

The benefit is most pronounced in: (a) low-data regimes where the model has
not seen enough examples to learn consistent labeling patterns implicitly;
(b) tasks with many entity types and complex tag schemes (BIOES); (c) when
the model is smaller or less capable.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Saying "BERT already captures dependencies, so CRF is unnecessary"
 without distinguishing input-side from output-side dependencies.
 
- Not knowing what a CRF transition matrix does.
 
- Being unable to explain what "invalid label sequences" means.
 
- Saying the CRF always helps—in practice, for large fine-tuned BERT
 models with abundant data, the improvement is often marginal.
questions.followups_source:
How is the CRF layer trained end-to-end with BERT? What is the
partition function and how is it computed? When does CRF not help?
What is the label bias problem?

questions.question:
What is perplexity? How does it relate to cross-entropy?
What are its limitations as an evaluation metric?
questions.say:
Perplexity is the exponential of the cross-entropy loss — the same quantity in different units. If you measure cross-entropy in bits, perplexity is two to that; in nats, e to that. A model at 3 nats has perplexity about twenty.

The intuition that makes it useful is effective branching factor: perplexity twenty means the model is on average about as uncertain as if it were choosing uniformly among twenty next words. Lower means it put more probability on what actually came next. A uniform model over a vocabulary of size V has perplexity exactly V — that's the do-nothing baseline.

The limitations matter more than the definition, and this is where the question usually goes. It's tokenizer-dependent, so two models with different vocabularies aren't comparable at all; if you have to compare across tokenizers you use bits per byte instead. It only measures local next-token prediction, so it says nothing about global coherence or whether the content is true. It's domain-specific — the same model can look excellent on news and terrible on clinical notes. And crucially it doesn't predict downstream capability: two models within noise of each other on perplexity can be far apart on QA or summarization, which is why nobody reports perplexity as a capability claim anymore. It's a training-health metric and a language-modeling comparison within a fixed tokenizer, and that's about it.
numbers: Uniform model over a vocabulary of size V has perplexity exactly V
red_flags: Not being able to state the relationship to cross-entropy.
Comparing perplexity across models with different tokenizers.
Claiming perplexity measures fluency, coherence, or factuality.
followups: What's the perplexity of a uniform model over vocabulary V?
How do you compute perplexity for a subword model?
Why doesn't a frontier model's perplexity tell you how good it is at reasoning?
questions.answer_source:
Perplexity measures how well a probabilistic language model predicts a test
set. It is defined as:
$\text{PP}(W) = \exp\!\bigl(-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N} \ln P(w_t \given w_1, \ldots, w_{t-1})\bigr)$,
which equals $2^{H(W)}$ where $H(W)$ is the cross-entropy per word.

Cross-entropy $H(W) = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_t \log_2 P(w_t \given \text{context})$
measures the average number of bits needed to encode each word under the model.
Perplexity is the exponentiation of this quantity, giving it an intuitive
interpretation as the weighted average number of equally likely next words the
model considers at each step. Lower perplexity means the model is more certain
and assigns higher probability to the actual words.

Limitations: (1) Perplexity is vocabulary-dependent—models with different
tokenizations are not directly comparable (use bits-per-byte for fair
comparison). (2) It only measures local next-token prediction, not global
coherence or factual correctness. (3) It is domain-specific—a model can
have excellent perplexity on news but poor perplexity on medical text. (4) It
does not predict downstream task performance: two models with similar perplexity
can differ substantially on QA or summarization.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Not knowing the formula or the connection to cross-entropy.
 
- Saying "lower perplexity is always better" without qualification.
 
- Claiming perplexity measures fluency, coherence, or factuality.
 
- Not knowing that perplexity is not comparable across different
 vocabularies or tokenizers.
questions.followups_source:
What is the perplexity of a uniform model over vocabulary $V$?
How do you compute perplexity for subword models? Why does GPT-4's
perplexity not tell us how good it is at reasoning?

questions.question: Explain the Word2Vec Skip-gram model. What is the training objective? What is negative sampling and why is it needed?
questions.answer_source:
Word2Vec Skip-gram learns word embeddings by training a model to predict
context words given a center word. Each word $w$ has two vectors: an input
embedding $\vw_w$ and an output embedding $\vw'_w$. Given center word $w_I$,
the probability of observing context word $w_O$ is:
\[
 P(w_O \given w_I)
 = \frac{\exp(\vw'_{w_O}{}^\top \vw_{w_I})}
 {\sum_{w=1}^{V} \exp(\vw'_w{}^\top \vw_{w_I})}
\]
The training objective maximizes the sum of $\log P(\text{context} \given
\text{center})$ over all (center, context) pairs in the corpus.

The problem is the denominator: it sums over the entire vocabulary $V$ (often
100K+ words) for every training example. Negative sampling replaces this
expensive softmax with a binary classification task. For each true
(center, context) pair, we sample $k$ noise words and train a binary
classifier to distinguish real pairs from noise. The loss becomes:
\[
 \loss = -\log\sigma(\vw'_{w_O}{}^\top \vw_{w_I})
 - \sum_{i=1}^{k} \E_{w_i \sim P_n}\bigl[
 \log\sigma(-\vw'_{w_i}{}^\top \vw_{w_I})\bigr]
\]
The noise distribution is the unigram distribution raised to the 3/4 power,
which smooths the distribution and makes negative samples more informative.
This reduces training from $O(V)$ to $O(k)$ per example.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Not knowing that Skip-gram has two sets of embeddings (input and
 output).
 
- Saying "negative sampling samples wrong words" without explaining
 the binary classification formulation.
 
- Being unable to explain why the 3/4 exponent on the noise
 distribution helps.
 
- Confusing Skip-gram (predict context from center) with CBOW
 (predict center from context).
questions.followups_source:
What is the connection between Word2Vec and PMI? How do you choose
the number of negative samples? What is subsampling and why does it help?
How does window size affect the type of relationships captured?
questions.say:
Skip-gram learns embeddings by predicting context words from a center word. Every word gets two vectors — an input vector used when it's the center, an output vector used when it's context — and that detail matters, because people forget it and then can't explain what gets shipped at the end, which is the input matrix. The objective is to maximize the log probability of the true context words, summed over every center-context pair in the corpus, where that probability is a softmax over the whole vocabulary.

The problem is that denominator. It sums over the entire vocabulary — a hundred thousand words or more — for every single training pair, so every gradient step touches every output vector. That's the entire reason negative sampling exists.

Negative sampling replaces the multi-class softmax with binary classification. For each real center-context pair you draw k noise words, and you train a logistic classifier to call the observed pair real and the noise pairs fake. That takes the per-example cost from order-vocabulary down to order-k. The one non-obvious piece is the noise distribution: it isn't the raw unigram distribution, it's unigram raised to the three-quarters power. That flattens it, so you draw rare words as negatives more often than their frequency warrants and get more informative gradients than if you sampled "the" over and over.
numbers: Negative sampling: O(V) → O(k) per example
Noise distribution: unigram raised to the 3/4 power
red_flags: Not knowing Skip-gram has two embedding matrices, input and output.
"Negative sampling just samples wrong words" without the binary-classification reformulation.
Confusing Skip-gram with CBOW — predict context from center, not the reverse.
followups: What's the connection between Word2Vec and PMI?
How do you choose the number of negative samples?
What is subsampling of frequent words and why does it help?

questions.question: What are the differences between Word2Vec, GloVe and FastText? When would you choose each one?
questions.answer_source:
All three produce static word embeddings but differ in their training approach
and capabilities.

**Word2Vec** (Mikolov et al., 2013) trains a shallow neural network on
local context windows. Skip-gram predicts context from center word; CBOW
predicts center from context. Training is online (streaming) and scales to
very large corpora. Limitation: treats words as atomic units, no OOV
handling.

**GloVe** (Pennington et al., 2014) first computes a global
co-occurrence matrix, then optimizes a weighted least-squares objective so
that word vector dot products approximate the log co-occurrence count. It
explicitly captures global statistics that Word2Vec's local windows might
miss, but requires pre-computing the co-occurrence matrix ($O(V^2)$ space,
though sparse in practice).

**FastText** (Bojanowski et al., 2017) extends Word2Vec by representing
each word as a bag of character n-grams. A word's vector is the sum of its
n-gram vectors. This enables OOV handling (decompose unseen words into known
n-grams), captures morphological structure, and produces better embeddings
for morphologically rich languages.

**When to choose each:**

 
- **Word2Vec:** General-purpose embeddings, very large corpora,
 when morphology is not a concern (e.g., English for well-curated text).
 
- **GloVe:** When you want pre-trained vectors (Stanford provides
 high-quality pre-trained GloVe), or when you specifically need embeddings
 that capture global co-occurrence patterns.
 
- **FastText:** Morphologically rich languages, noisy text
 (social media, user-generated content with typos), specialized domains
 with many OOV terms. Also when you need fast supervised classification
 (FastText's supervised mode).

In practice, for most modern systems, the choice between these three matters
less than whether to use them at all versus a contextual model. But for
low-resource, low-latency, or edge-deployment scenarios, FastText remains a
strong choice.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Saying "they are all the same, just use BERT."
 
- Not knowing that GloVe uses a global co-occurrence matrix while
 Word2Vec uses local windows.
 
- Not knowing that FastText handles OOV via character n-grams.
 
- Being unable to articulate when static embeddings are preferred
 over contextual ones.
questions.followups_source:
How does Levy and Goldberg's result connect Word2Vec to SVD on
a PMI matrix? When would you use static embeddings in a modern system?
How does FastText's approach differ from BPE tokenization?
questions.say:
All three give you one static vector per word. They differ in what they train on and whether they can handle a word they've never seen.

Word2Vec trains a shallow network on local context windows - skip-gram predicts context from the center word, CBOW does the reverse. It streams, so it scales to enormous corpora, but words are atomic: an unseen word has no vector at all.

GloVe goes the other way. It builds the global co-occurrence matrix first, then fits vectors so dot products approximate log co-occurrence counts, using corpus-wide statistics directly rather than hoping local windows aggregate to them. The cost is materializing that matrix, and it's equally helpless on out-of-vocabulary words.

FastText is Word2Vec plus character n-grams: a word's vector is the sum of its subword n-gram vectors. That gives you OOV handling for free and captures morphology, which matters a great deal in inflected languages.

So FastText for typos, user-generated text, morphologically rich languages, or heavy domain vocabulary; GloVe if I just want good pretrained English vectors off the shelf. But the bigger decision is whether static embeddings are right at all - a contextual model beats all three when you can afford it, and static vectors earn their place on latency, memory and edge deployment.
red_flags: "They're all the same, just use BERT" - dodges the question and misses where static vectors still win.
Doesn't know GloVe uses global co-occurrence counts while Word2Vec uses local windows.
Doesn't know FastText gets OOV handling from character n-grams.
followups: How does Levy and Goldberg's result connect Word2Vec to SVD on a PMI matrix?
When would you use static embeddings in a system today?
How is FastText's n-gram decomposition different from BPE?

questions.question: Why are contextual embeddings better than static embeddings? Give a concrete example of when static embeddings fail.
questions.say:
Because a static embedding has to give one vector to a word that means several different things, and that vector is a compromise that is wrong for every sense.

The clean example is "crane". The crane lifted the steel beam - construction equipment. We saw a crane at the lake - a bird. She had to crane her neck - a verb meaning to stretch. Word2Vec or GloVe puts all three at a single point, somewhere in the average of machinery, wildlife and body movement, which is a location that describes none of them. A contextual model gives you three different vectors, and it does word-sense disambiguation for free, without anyone building a sense inventory.

Polysemy is the headline but not the whole story. Contextual models also encode syntactic role - "running" as a noun and as a verb come out differently - and sentence-level effects like negation and quantification propagate into the token representations, which static vectors have no mechanism for at all.

The empirical jump was large: BERT moved GLUE up by roughly seven points over the previous state of the art, which is not a normal increment on that benchmark.

I would not say static embeddings are dead, though. They are extremely cheap, they make honest baselines, and they are still fine inside larger systems where you need a fast lookup rather than a forward pass.
numbers: BERT: ~7 points absolute on GLUE over the previous state of the art
red_flags: "Contextual is better because BERT is better" with no mechanism.
No concrete polysemy example when asked for one.
Claiming static embeddings are useless today.
followups: What do ELMo's different layers capture?
How does BERT build context differently from ELMo?
Where would you still use static embeddings today?
questions.notes: Source says BERT improved GLUE "by 7+ points over ELMo". The 7.7-point figure in the BERT paper is against the previous state of the art (OpenAI GPT), not against ELMo, whose gap is larger. Reworded to "over the previous state of the art".
questions.answer_source:
Static embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe, FastText) assign a single fixed vector to
each word regardless of context. Contextual embeddings (ELMo, BERT) assign
**different** vectors depending on the surrounding words.

The fundamental failure mode of static embeddings is **polysemy**.
Consider the word "crane":

 
- "The **crane** lifted the steel beam." (construction
 equipment)
 
- "We observed a **crane** at the lake." (bird)
 
- "She had to **crane** her neck to see." (verb: to stretch)

A static embedding places all three senses at a single point—a compromise
that accurately represents none of them. A contextual model produces three
distinct vectors, each appropriate for its context.

Beyond polysemy, contextual embeddings capture:

 
- **Word sense disambiguation** (automatically, without explicit
 sense inventories).
 
- **Syntactic role** ("running" as noun vs.\ verb gets
 different representations).
 
- **Sentence-level semantics** (negation, quantification,
 conditionals affect word representations).

Quantitatively, the shift from static to contextual embeddings produced
massive improvements: BERT improved GLUE benchmark scores by 7+ points over
ELMo (which itself improved significantly over static embeddings).
questions.red_flags_source:
- Giving only "contextual is better because BERT is better" without
 explaining the polysemy problem.
 
- Not being able to give a concrete example.
 
- Saying static embeddings are "useless" (they are still useful
 for efficiency, baselines, and as components of larger systems).
questions.followups_source:
What does ELMo capture at different layers? How does BERT create
contextual embeddings differently from ELMo? When would you still use static
embeddings in a modern system?

questions.question: Your new embedding model wins offline — +4 points Recall@100 on your evaluation set — but loses the online A/B test. Walk me through your investigation.
questions.say:
I'd treat this as two measurements that disagree and enumerate what differs between them, cheapest and most likely first — and the highest-prior cause usually isn't the model, it's latency. If a much larger encoder replaced a small one, twenty to forty milliseconds of extra query latency will cost more engagement than four points of Recall@100 buys. So I check per-arm latency distributions and guardrail metrics, and confirm the test is bucketed and powered, before touching relevance at all.

Next, serving parity. Was the entire corpus re-embedded? A partially backfilled index fails silently and catastrophically, because vectors from two different models aren't comparable — the un-migrated slice just scores as noise. Then check preprocessing: many of these models expect a query prefix or instruction, and if the offline eval had it and serving doesn't, the advantage is gone.

Third, the ANN interaction. Offline you almost certainly scored with exact search, while production serves from HNSW or IVF-PQ tuned on the old model's geometry. Measure ANN-versus-exact overlap at 100 in both arms and retune the index before judging the model.

Fourth, downstream coupling — a reranker or click model trained on the old candidate distribution can mis-score unfamiliar candidates, converting better recall into worse final rankings. Only then would I question the plus-four itself: stale eval sets, and click labels carrying position and selection bias toward whatever the old system surfaced.
red_flags: "The A/B is underpowered, ship it anyway" — or the reverse, "offline metrics are meaningless"
Not knowing that two models' embeddings can't share one index
Never considering latency, or assuming production search is exact rather than ANN
followups: How would you retune HNSW for a new embedding distribution?
How do you get unbiased relevance labels out of click logs?
Retrain the reranker before or during the embedder A/B?
questions.answer_source:
I would treat this as a discrepancy between two measurements and
systematically enumerate what differs between the offline eval and the
online system, ordered by cheapness to check and prior probability.

**1.\ Validate the experiment itself.** Before debugging the model:
is the A/B correctly bucketed, adequately powered, and are guardrail
metrics clean? The single most common culprit is **latency**: if the
new model is larger (say a 7B decoder replacing a 110M encoder), an extra
20–40ms per query degrades engagement enough to swamp a $+4$ Recall gain.
Check latency distributions per arm first—a relevance win inside a
latency loss is a launch-blocking but perfectly diagnosable state.

**2.\ Check serving parity with the offline eval.** The offline
pipeline and the serving path must run the **same** model the same way:

 
- **Mixed embedding spaces:** if the corpus backfill was
 incomplete, some documents in the new index still carry old-model
 vectors. Embedding spaces from different models are mutually
 incomparable, so a partially backfilled index fails silently and
 catastrophically for the un-migrated slice.
 
- **Prompt/preprocessing mismatch:** missing
 `query:`~/ instruction prefixes at serving time (while the
 offline eval used them), different truncation lengths, or a missing
 normalization step will quietly destroy the model's advantage.

**3.\ ANN–recall interaction.** Offline evals typically score with
exact (brute-force) search; production serves from an ANN index (HNSW,
IVF-PQ) whose parameters were tuned on the **old** model's geometry.
A new embedder changes norm distributions and cluster structure, so the
same `efSearch`/`nprobe` settings can yield materially lower
ANN recall on the new vectors. Measure ANN-vs-exact overlap@100 in both
arms; if the new arm's ANN recall is lower, retune the index before judging
the model.

**4.\ Downstream coupling.** The first-stage embedder does not act
alone: a re-ranker or click model trained on the old candidate distribution
may mis-score the new, unfamiliar candidates, converting better recall into
worse final rankings. The clean test is to retrain (or at least
recalibrate) the re-ranker on candidates from the new model before the A/B.

**5.\ Interrogate the offline labels.** The $+4$ itself may be
partly artifactual. Eval sets go **stale**: if queries and labels
were harvested months ago, the offline win is measured on yesterday's
query and document distribution, not the live one. And labels derived
from logged clicks carry **position bias** and selection bias: they
over-represent documents the **old** system surfaced and users could
see, so offline deltas computed on them are untrustworthy in both
directions. If the labels came from an LLM judge, audit for systematic
preferences correlated with the new model's training data. Slice both
offline and online metrics by query segment (head vs.\ tail, navigational
vs.\ exploratory) to find where the online loss concentrates, and use
interleaving for a more sensitive online ranking comparison.

In practice the highest-prior causes are, in order: latency regression,
missing instruction/prefix parity, incomplete re-embedding, and un-retuned
ANN parameters—all checkable in a day, and all more likely than "the
offline metric was simply wrong."
questions.red_flags_source:
- Concluding "the A/B must be underpowered—ship it anyway,"
 or conversely "offline metrics are meaningless." Both measurements
 are information; the job is reconciling them.
 
- Not knowing that embeddings from two different models cannot
 coexist in one index.
 
- Never mentioning latency as a confound.
 
- Assuming production search is exact—not knowing the offline
 eval used brute force while serving uses ANN.
 
- No awareness that click-derived labels are position- and
 selection-biased.
questions.followups_source:
How would you retune an HNSW index for a new embedding
distribution? How do you collect unbiased relevance labels from click
logs? Would you retrain the re-ranker before or during the embedder A/B?
At what point do you abandon the new model versus keep debugging the
serving stack?

questions.question:
Explain the vanishing gradient problem in RNNs. Why does LSTM
solve it? Walk through the math.
questions.say:
In a vanilla RNN, backpropagating from step t back to step k means multiplying together t minus k Jacobians, and each is the recurrent weight matrix times a diagonal of tanh derivatives. Tanh's derivative is at most one and usually well below it, so unless the recurrent matrix's largest singular value compensates, that product shrinks geometrically. Ten or twenty steps back and the gradient is numerically zero — the network cannot learn a dependency at that range no matter how long you train. Push the singular value the other way and you get the mirror problem, exploding gradients.

The LSTM fix is structural, not "it has gates." It adds a cell state updated by addition: new cell equals forget gate times old cell, plus input gate times the candidate. Because that path is additive and the gating is elementwise, the derivative of the cell at time t with respect to the cell at time k is a product of diagonal matrices of forget-gate values — no repeated multiplication by a weight matrix at all. With the forget gate near one, that product is roughly the identity and gradient flows essentially unattenuated across arbitrary distance.

I wouldn't overclaim: this mitigates the problem, it doesn't remove it. Forget gates below one still decay, just gracefully rather than geometrically through a matrix. It's the same trick as a ResNet skip connection — an identity path so the gradient has a route that isn't multiplied down.
red_flags: "LSTMs have gates so they solve it" with no account of why — the additive path and the diagonal Jacobian are the answer.
Confusing vanishing gradients with small activations.
Claiming LSTMs eliminate the problem rather than mitigate it.
followups: How does gradient clipping help with the exploding case?
Compare this to ResNet skip connections.
Do transformers have a vanishing gradient problem?
questions.answer_source:
In a vanilla RNN, the gradient of a loss at time $t$ with respect to
parameters at time $k$ involves a product of Jacobians
$\prod_{j=k+1}^{t} \frac{\partial \vh_j}{\partial \vh_{j-1}}$.
Each Jacobian is
$\diag(\tanh'(\cdot)) \cdot \mW_h$,
where $\tanh'(z) \in (0, 1]$. If the largest singular value of $\mW_h$
is less than $1/\gamma$ (with $\gamma \leq 1$ bounding the derivative),
this product decays **exponentially** as $(t - k)$ grows. After even 10–20
steps, the gradient is effectively zero, making it impossible to learn
long-range dependencies.

LSTM solves this by introducing a cell state $\vc_t$ updated via
**addition**: $\vc_t = \mathbf{f}_t \odot \vc_{t-1} +
\mathbf{i}_t \odot \tilde{\vc}_t$. The gradient
$\partial \vc_t / \partial \vc_k$ reduces to a product of
**diagonal** matrices $\prod \diag(\mathbf{f}_j)$. When the forget
gate is near 1, this product is approximately the identity matrix—the
gradient flows perfectly across arbitrary distances. The key structural
change is replacing matrix multiplication with element-wise gating over
an additive cell state.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Saying "LSTM has gates so it solves vanishing gradients" without
 explaining **why** gates help (additive path, diagonal Jacobian).

- Confusing vanishing gradients with small activations.

- Claiming LSTMs **completely** eliminate the problem (they
 mitigate it; very long sequences can still be difficult).

- Not mentioning the spectral norm bound or the mathematical mechanism.
questions.followups_source:
How does gradient clipping help with exploding gradients?
Compare the LSTM solution to ResNet skip connections. Does the vanishing
gradient problem affect transformers?

questions.question: Walk me through the LSTM cell gate by gate. What is each gate's purpose?
questions.answer_source:
An LSTM has three gates and a cell candidate, all operating on the
concatenation $[\vh_{t-1}, \vx_t]$:

(1)~The **forget gate** $\mathbf{f}_t = \sigma(\mW_f [\vh_{t-1},
\vx_t] + \vb_f)$ decides what to **erase** from the cell state.
Each element in $[0,1]$ controls whether to keep or discard that
dimension of memory.

(2)~The **input gate** $\mathbf{i}_t = \sigma(\mW_i [\vh_{t-1},
\vx_t] + \vb_i)$ decides what new information to **write**.

(3)~The **cell candidate** $\tilde{\vc}_t = \tanh(\mW_c [\vh_{t-1},
\vx_t] + \vb_c)$ proposes new content in $[-1, 1]$.

The cell state updates as
$\vc_t = \mathbf{f}_t \odot \vc_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t \odot \tilde{\vc}_t$—
an additive combination of gated old memory and gated new content.

(4)~The **output gate** $\mathbf{o}_t = \sigma(\mW_o [\vh_{t-1},
\vx_t] + \vb_o)$ controls which parts of the cell state are exposed as
the hidden state $\vh_t = \mathbf{o}_t \odot \tanh(\vc_t)$.

The cell state is the long-term memory that can persist unchanged; the
hidden state is the short-term, filtered view that other layers see.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Listing gates without explaining their purpose or interaction.

- Getting the order of operations wrong (e.g., applying output gate
 before cell update).

- Forgetting the $\tanh$ on $\vc_t$ in the hidden state equation.

- Not distinguishing cell state from hidden state.
questions.followups_source:
What is the parameter count of an LSTM layer? How should you
initialize the forget gate bias and why? Compare LSTM to GRU.
questions.say:
Three gates and a candidate, and all four read the same thing: the previous hidden state concatenated with the current input.

The forget gate is a sigmoid, so it's between zero and one per dimension, and it decides what to erase from the cell state — one means keep this memory slot, zero means wipe it. The input gate, also a sigmoid, decides how much new information to write. The cell candidate is a tanh, so it's between minus one and one, and it proposes what that new content actually is. Then the cell update is the whole point: new cell state equals old cell state times the forget gate, plus the candidate times the input gate. It's additive, not a repeated matrix multiply, so the gradient path along the cell state doesn't shrink geometrically the way a vanilla RNN's does — that's the entire reason the architecture exists.

The output gate then decides which parts of the cell state get exposed. The hidden state is the output gate times tanh of the cell state — and note that tanh, people drop it when they write it out.

The distinction I'd emphasize is cell state versus hidden state. The cell is long-term memory that can pass through many timesteps essentially unchanged; the hidden state is the filtered short-term view that the next layer and the next timestep actually see.
red_flags: Listing the gates without saying what each one is for or how they interact.
Getting the order wrong — applying the output gate before the cell update.
Dropping the tanh on the cell state in the hidden-state equation.
Not distinguishing cell state from hidden state.

questions.question: Why did transformers replace LSTMs? What specific limitations did they address?
questions.answer_source:
Transformers replaced LSTMs by addressing three fundamental limitations:

**(1) Sequential computation.** An LSTM processes tokens one at a
time—$\vh_t$ depends on $\vh_{t-1}$. This creates an $O(T)$ sequential
bottleneck that cannot be parallelized across time steps. Transformers
use self-attention, where every token attends to every other token
**simultaneously**, enabling full parallelism on GPUs/TPUs. This
difference makes transformers dramatically faster to train.

**(2) Long-range dependency path length.** In an LSTM, information
from position 1 must traverse all intermediate hidden states to reach
position $T$—a path of length $O(T)$. Even with the cell state, some
degradation occurs. In a transformer, any two positions are connected
by a **direct** attention path of length $O(1)$, making long-range
dependencies much easier to capture.

**(3) Scalability.** LSTMs do not benefit proportionally from
larger models and datasets. Transformers exhibit favorable
**scaling laws**: performance improves predictably as a power law
with compute, data, and parameters. This enabled the scale-up from
BERT (340M) to GPT-3 (175B) to modern frontier models.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Saying "transformers are just better" without explaining why.

- Forgetting the parallelization advantage (the most important
 practical reason).

- Not mentioning path length for long-range dependencies.

- Claiming LSTMs are completely obsolete (they still have niche uses).
questions.followups_source:
What is the computational complexity of self-attention?
Where might you still use an LSTM today? What are the limitations of
transformers that LSTMs do not have?
questions.say:
Three reasons, and the first is the one that actually decided it: parallelism. An LSTM's hidden state at step t depends on step t minus one, so training is a sequential chain as long as the sequence and you simply can't use the hardware. Self-attention computes all positions at once, so a training step is a few large matrix multiplies that saturate a GPU. That's orders of magnitude in wall-clock, and it's what made scaling possible at all.

Second, path length. In an LSTM, information from position one reaches position T through every intermediate state, degrading along the way even with the gating. In a transformer any two positions are one attention hop apart, so a long-range dependency doesn't have to survive the journey.

Third, and downstream of the first two, scaling behavior. Transformers keep improving predictably as you add parameters, data and compute - that's what the scaling laws describe - while LSTMs plateau. Once that was visible everything followed: BERT at a few hundred million, GPT-3 at 175 billion.

What you give up is the constant-size state. Attention is quadratic in sequence length where an LSTM step is O(1) in memory, which is genuinely better for streaming and very long inputs, and it's why constant-state architectures keep resurfacing.
numbers: Attention is O(n^2) in sequence length; an LSTM step is O(1) state
red_flags: "Transformers are just better" with no mechanism.
Leads with attention quality and never mentions parallel training, which is the practical reason.
Claims LSTMs are entirely obsolete; constant-state models still win on streaming and very long inputs.

questions.question: Explain the attention mechanism in seq2seq. Why was it needed?
questions.say:
Attention was needed because the original seq2seq model funnels the entire source sentence through one fixed-size vector, and that is an information bottleneck. The decoder has to reconstruct everything it needs about a fifty-word sentence from the encoder's last hidden state, and performance fell off as sentences got longer - exactly the symptom you would predict.

Bahdanau's fix was to stop making the decoder live off one summary. At each decoding step, the decoder scores its current state against every encoder hidden state, softmaxes those scores into weights, and takes a weighted sum of the encoder states as its context. So the context is recomputed for every output token and can look at whichever part of the source is relevant right now.

Three things fall out of that. The decoder gets the full encoder sequence rather than a lossy summary. The weights learn alignment - for translation you can plot them and read off a soft word alignment, which was a genuinely nice interpretability result at the time. And gradients get a much shorter path back to early encoder states, because attention is a direct connection rather than a walk back through every recurrent step.

The scoring function is either additive, a small MLP over the two states, or multiplicative, a bilinear dot product. Multiplicative is cheaper, and it is the one that survives into Transformer attention.
red_flags: Conflating seq2seq cross-attention with Transformer self-attention.
Never naming the fixed-vector bottleneck that motivated it.
"The model pays attention to important words" with no mechanism - no scores, no softmax, no weighted sum.
followups: Additive versus multiplicative scoring - what is the difference?
How does Transformer cross-attention relate to this?
What does attention cost computationally?
questions.answer_source:
In a basic seq2seq model, the encoder compresses the entire input
sequence into a single fixed-size context vector $\vc = \vh_T^e$. For
long sequences, this creates an **information bottleneck**—the
decoder must reconstruct all relevant source information from one vector.

Attention (Bahdanau et al., 2015) solves this by allowing the decoder at
each step $t$ to compute a dynamic weighted sum of **all** encoder
hidden states:
$\vc_t = \sum_i \alpha_{t,i} \vh_i^e$,
where $\alpha_{t,i} = \softmax(\text{score}(\vh_t^d, \vh_i^e))$.

The scoring function can be additive
($\mathbf{v}^T \tanh(\mW_1 \vh_t^d + \mW_2 \vh_i^e)$)
or multiplicative ($(\vh_t^d)^T \mW \vh_i^e$).

This is powerful because: (a) the decoder accesses the full encoder
sequence, not a lossy summary; (b) the attention weights learn to
**align** output positions with relevant input positions; and (c) it
creates shorter gradient paths from decoder loss to encoder states
(attention weights provide a direct connection).
questions.red_flags_source:
- Confusing seq2seq attention with self-attention in transformers.

- Not explaining the information bottleneck that motivated attention.

- Describing attention as "the model pays attention to important
 words" without any mathematical substance.

questions.question: Explain self-attention step by step, including the math.
questions.say:
Every token produces three vectors from the same input through three learned projections — a query, a key and a value. The query is what this position is looking for, the key is what a position advertises, and the value is what it hands over if it gets selected. Keeping them separate matters: it lets a position attend on one basis and retrieve something else, which a single shared projection couldn't do.

You dot each query against every key, giving an n-by-n matrix of compatibility scores, then divide by the square root of the head dimension. That scaling isn't cosmetic — the dot product of two random vectors has variance proportional to dimension, so at 128 dimensions raw scores are large, the softmax saturates toward one-hot, and gradients vanish. Scaling keeps the logits order one at initialization. Then you softmax each row, so the weights over positions are non-negative and sum to one, and use them to take a weighted average of the value vectors. Causal masking is just setting the future positions to negative infinity before the softmax.

Cost is quadratic in sequence length: n-squared times d compute, and naively n-squared memory for the score matrix — though that memory term is what FlashAttention removes by tiling and never materializing the full matrix. Multi-head is all of this done in parallel in several lower-dimensional subspaces, then concatenated.
numbers: Attention is O(n²d) compute; O(n²) attention-matrix memory unless tiled (FlashAttention)
red_flags: Can't write the formula when handed the marker
Omitting the 1/√d_k scale, or unable to say why it exists
"It's just a weighted average" with no account of where the weights come from
followups: How does causal masking change the computation?
Where does the memory saving in FlashAttention come from?
What is the relationship between attention and convolution?
questions.whiteboard: $\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$ — write it once, then point at each piece as you talk: $QK^\top$ is an n×n score matrix, one row per query; $\sqrt{d_k}$ is variance control so the softmax doesn't saturate; the output is a convex combination of the value vectors.
questions.notes: Source stated attention memory as O(n²) without qualification; say notes that FlashAttention avoids materializing the n×n matrix, which is the expected follow-up at L5+.
questions.answer_source:
Given input $\mX \in \R^{n \times d}$, we compute three projections:
$\mQ = \mX\mW_Q$, $\mK = \mX\mW_K$, $\mV = \mX\mW_V$. The attention output
is $\softmax(\mQ\mK^\top / \sqrt{d_k})\,\mV$. The QK dot product computes
pairwise compatibility scores. We scale by $\sqrt{d_k}$ because the dot
product variance grows with $d_k$, which would saturate the softmax. After
softmax normalization (row-wise), each position gets a weighted combination of
all value vectors, where the weights reflect relevance. Separate Q/K/V
projections allow attending based on one aspect while retrieving another.
Complexity is $O(n^2 d)$ compute and $O(n^2)$ memory for the attention matrix.

- Confuses self-attention with cross-attention

- Says "attention is just a weighted average" without explaining how

questions.question: Why do we scale by $\sqrt{d_k}$? Derive the variance argument.
questions.say:
Because without it the dot products grow with dimension and drive softmax into saturation.

Take queries and keys with independent, unit-variance entries. The dot product is a sum of d_k products, each with mean zero and variance one, so the sum has variance d_k and standard deviation root d_k. At head dimension 64, that's a standard deviation of 8, so typical logits span roughly plus or minus 24. Softmax over a range that wide is effectively one-hot: one entry takes everything, the rest get numerically nothing.

That's fatal for training, not just for the forward pass, because the gradient of softmax goes like p times one minus p. Saturate it and the gradient goes to zero — the attention weights stop moving and the layer stops learning where to look. Dividing by root d_k puts the variance back at one regardless of head dimension, which keeps softmax in the region where it has usable gradient.

The cleanest way to think about it is temperature. Root d_k is a temperature chosen so that a 64-dimensional head and a 128-dimensional head behave identically at initialization, which is what lets you change head dimension without retuning anything.

And I'd add that it isn't a permanent fix: the argument only holds at initialization, and logits genuinely do drift upward over a long run, which is exactly why modern large models add QK-norm or soft-capping on top of the scaling.
numbers: d_k = 64: raw dot-product std ~= 8, so logits span roughly +/-24 before scaling
red_flags: "It normalizes the values" with no quantitative argument.
Can't show that the dot-product variance is d_k.
Confusing this with layer normalization.
followups: What happens if you use a different scaling factor?
What's the relationship between this and softmax temperature?

questions.answer_source:
Assume $q_i, k_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ i.i.d. The dot product
$\vq^\top\vk = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i$ has mean 0 and variance
$\Var(\vq^\top\vk) = \sum_i \Var(q_i k_i) = \sum_i \E[q_i^2]\E[k_i^2] = d_k$.
So the standard deviation is $\sqrt{d_k}$. For $d_k = 64$, raw dot products
have std $\approx 8$. The softmax of values in range $[-24, 24]$ is
essentially one-hot, producing vanishing gradients. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$
normalizes the variance back to 1, keeping softmax in its sensitive region.

- "It normalizes the values" without quantitative reasoning
 
- Cannot derive that the variance equals $d_k$
 
- Confuses this with layer normalization

relationship between scaling and softmax temperature?

questions.question: Why do we need multiple attention heads? What happens with just one head?
questions.answer_source:
A single head can capture only one attention pattern per layer. Multiple heads
allow parallel attention in different representation subspaces: one head might
track syntactic dependencies (subject-verb), another positional adjacency,
another semantic similarity. Each head projects into $d_k = d/h$ dimensions
with independent $\mW_Q^{(i)}, \mW_K^{(i)}, \mW_V^{(i)}$. The output
projection $\mW_O$ mixes information across heads. Computationally, multi-head
costs the same as single-head at full dimension because the total dimension is
split across heads. Empirically, single-head attention at full dimension
performs significantly worse, especially on tasks requiring diverse reasoning.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Cannot explain what "different subspaces" means concretely
 
- Thinks multi-head attention is more expensive than single-head
 
- Does not mention the output projection $\mW_O$ and its role
questions.followups_source:
How would you determine which heads are important? Can you prune
attention heads? What is the effect of head dimension on performance?
questions.say:
One head can only express one attention pattern per layer — a single softmax distribution over positions for each query. Multiple heads let the layer attend in several representation subspaces at once: one head tracking syntactic dependencies like subject-verb, another doing something close to positional adjacency, another semantic similarity. You get several relationships per token instead of a weighted compromise between them.

The cost argument is the part people get backwards. Multi-head isn't more expensive than single-head at the same model dimension, because you split the dimension across heads — each head projects into d over h dimensions with its own query, key and value projections, so total QKV compute is unchanged. You're not buying capacity, you're buying diversity out of capacity you already had.

The output projection is what makes it a single layer rather than h disjoint ones. Each head produces its own d-over-h output, they're concatenated, and W_O mixes across them so downstream layers see one combined representation. Leave that out and the heads can never interact.

Empirically, single-head attention at full dimension performs significantly worse, and the gap widens on tasks that need several kinds of relationship resolved at the same time.
numbers: Each head projects into d/h dimensions, so h heads cost the same as one full-width head
red_flags: Can't say concretely what "different subspaces" means.
Thinking multi-head attention costs more than single-head at the same model dimension.
Never mentioning the output projection W_O and what it does.

questions.question: Compare encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder transformers. Why did decoder-only dominate the LLM era?
questions.answer_source:
**Encoder-only** (BERT): bidirectional attention, trained with MLM, excels
at understanding/classification tasks but cannot generate text natively.
**Decoder-only** (GPT): causal attention, trained autoregressively,
natural for generation and showed emergent in-context learning at scale.
**Encoder-decoder** (T5): bidirectional encoder feeds into causal decoder
via cross-attention, strong for structured input-output tasks like translation.

Decoder-only dominated because: (1)~architectural simplicity—one stack, not
two; (2)~CLM scales naturally with internet-scale data; (3)~in-context learning
emerged, eliminating the need for task-specific fine-tuning; (4)~KV-cache
works cleanly for causal models—previously computed KVs never change.
Encoder-decoder still wins for some structured tasks but decoder-only's
flexibility and scaling properties proved decisive.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Cannot articulate the attention masking difference
 
- Says "GPT is better than BERT" without nuance
 
- Does not mention in-context learning as a key factor
 
- Confuses training objectives (MLM vs.\ CLM)
questions.followups_source:
When would you still choose BERT over an LLM? What is prefix
language modeling? Could encoder-decoder make a comeback?
questions.say:
Three shapes, and the difference is entirely in the attention mask and the training objective. Encoder-only, meaning BERT, is bidirectional: every token sees every other token, trained with masked language modeling. Great for classification and understanding, but it can't generate natively. Decoder-only, meaning GPT, is causal: each token sees only what came before it, trained to predict the next token. Encoder-decoder, meaning T5, has a bidirectional encoder feeding a causal decoder through cross-attention, which suits structured input-to-output tasks like translation.

Decoder-only won for four reasons. It's one stack instead of two, so there's less to build and less to tune. Next-token prediction scales cleanly on raw internet text - no masking scheme to design, no paired data to collect. In-context learning emerged from it at scale, which meant you stopped needing a separately fine-tuned model per task. And the KV cache works cleanly under causal masking, because previously computed keys and values never change, which is what makes serving tractable.

Encoder-decoder still wins on some structured tasks where you genuinely have a fixed input to condition on, and encoder-only models are still the right call for high-throughput classification and embeddings, where you don't need generation and you do want bidirectional context.
red_flags: Can't state the attention masking difference; that is the whole distinction.
"GPT is better than BERT" with no task framing.
Never mentions in-context learning as the reason per-task fine-tuning stopped mattering.

questions.question: What is the computational complexity of self-attention? Why is it a problem?
questions.say:
Self-attention is O(n squared times d) in compute and O(n squared) in memory if you materialise the score matrix - quadratic in sequence length, linear in model dimension. It comes from the Q-K-transpose product, which is n-by-d against d-by-n and gives you an n-by-n matrix, and then multiplying that by V costs the same again.

The reason it is a problem is that doubling the context quadruples both compute and memory. Put a real number on it: at 128K context with 32 heads, the attention matrix alone in float16 is about a terabyte. There is no GPU where that fits, which is why long-context models cannot just be the naive implementation.

There are three ways out and they differ in kind. Flash Attention is exact - it tiles the computation and never writes the n-by-n matrix out to HBM, so memory drops to linear in n while the compute stays quadratic. That is the one to name first, because it costs you nothing in quality. Then there are architectural changes that actually change the maths: sliding-window attention gets you to n times window size by attending only locally, and linear attention schemes get to order n-d by reordering the products, both at some approximation cost.

So the honest framing is that Flash Attention fixed the memory wall, not the compute wall. The quadratic FLOPs are still there at long context.
numbers: 128K context, 32 heads, float16: the attention matrix alone is ~1 TB
Attention: O(n^2 d) compute, O(n^2) memory naive, O(n) memory with Flash Attention
red_flags: Says linear, or cannot state O(n^2) at all.
Conflates compute complexity with memory complexity - Flash Attention fixes one, not the other.
No connection to why context length is capped in practice.
followups: How does Flash Attention get to O(n) memory?
What do you give up with linear attention?
How does Mamba compare?
questions.answer_source:
The $\mQ\mK^\top$ product is $\R^{n \times d_k} \cdot \R^{d_k \times n} = \R^{n \times n}$,
requiring $O(n^2 d_k)$ FLOPs. The subsequent multiplication with $\mV$ is also
$O(n^2 d_v)$. Total: $O(n^2 d)$ compute and $O(n^2 + nd)$ memory. For a
128K-token context with 32 heads, the attention matrix alone is
$32 \times 128\text{K}^2 \times 2$ bytes $\approx$ 1\,TB in float16—clearly
impractical without optimizations like Flash Attention (which reduces memory to
$O(n)$ without approximation) or architectural changes like sliding window
attention ($O(nw)$) or linear attention ($O(nd)$). The quadratic scaling means
doubling context length quadruples both compute and memory, fundamentally
limiting the sequences transformers can process.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Says "linear complexity" or cannot state $O(n^2)$
 
- Confuses compute complexity with memory complexity
 
- Does not connect to practical implications (context length limits)
questions.followups_source:
