tradeoffs of linear attention? How does Mamba compare?

questions.question: Explain BERT's pretraining objectives. Why was NSP removed in RoBERTa?
questions.say:
BERT trained on two objectives at once. Masked language modelling selects 15 percent of tokens and predicts them from both directions; of those selected positions, 80 percent are replaced with the mask token, 10 percent with a random token, and 10 percent left unchanged. That 80/10/10 split exists because the mask token never appears at fine-tuning time — if the model only ever had to reconstruct positions flagged with a special token, it would learn to do nothing at unflagged positions, so the random and unchanged cases force it to keep a useful representation everywhere.

Next sentence prediction was the second objective: given two segments, decide whether they're consecutive. RoBERTa removed it and got consistently better results. The explanation is that it's trivially easy — the negatives came from a different document, so topic overlap alone solves it and the model never has to learn discourse coherence. You spend capacity and part of every batch on a task with almost no signal.

Worth adding that RoBERTa's other changes probably mattered more than dropping NSP: dynamic masking rather than one mask pattern baked in at preprocessing, much larger batches, and 160 gigabytes of text against BERT's 16. The real headline of that paper is that BERT was simply undertrained.
red_flags: Saying 15 percent of tokens are replaced with [MASK] — 15 percent are selected, 80 percent of those masked
Can't explain why the 80/10/10 split exists
Doesn't know RoBERTa dropped NSP, or can't say why it was a weak objective

questions.answer_source:
BERT uses two pretraining objectives: (1)~**MLM**: 15\
selected; of those, 80\
The model predicts original tokens from bidirectional context. The 80/10/10
split prevents mismatch between pretraining (where `[MASK]` appears)
and fine-tuning (where it does not). (2)~**NSP**: binary prediction of
whether two sentences are consecutive. RoBERTa showed NSP hurts by removing
it and achieving consistently better results. The likely reasons: NSP is a
trivially easy task (topic matching suffices), it wastes model capacity on a
useless signal, and the "random sentence" negatives are too easy (different
documents = different topics). RoBERTa also found that dynamic masking
(re-masking each epoch), larger batch sizes, and much more training data
(160GB vs.\ 16GB) significantly improved results—BERT was simply
undertrained.

questions.question: When would you use LoRA vs.\ full fine-tuning? When would LoRA fail?
questions.say:
LoRA by default at 7B and up; full fine-tuning when the update you actually need is large.

The case for LoRA is mostly memory. You're not storing Adam's moment tensors for every parameter, which is what really blows out the GPU, so you can fine-tune a 7B on hardware that couldn't hold a full fine-tune, and you can run bigger batches. Be honest about wall-clock — maybe 1.2 to 1.5 times faster, not ten, because you still do a full backward pass through the frozen network. The other real win is serving: one base model resident, dozens of small adapters swapped per task.

Full fine-tuning when quality is the only constraint and you have the budget, when the model is small enough to be cheap anyway — under a billion, say — or when you're doing continued pretraining rather than task adaptation.

LoRA fails when the required update is genuinely high-rank, which happens when the target distribution is far from pretraining and the model has to unlearn and relearn rather than nudge. Adding a new language is the canonical case, partly because it also needs the embedding and tokenizer to move, and LoRA on attention projections doesn't touch those. It also fails at a rank too low for the task, where you've simply starved the adapter.

This question is really about data volume, GPU budget, and how many tasks you serve off one base — not about which knob you set.
numbers: LoRA wall-clock speedup ~1.2-1.5x; the dominant saving is optimizer-state memory, not time
red_flags: "Always use LoRA" or "always full fine-tune" with no conditions attached.
No concrete scenario where LoRA fails.
Claiming a large wall-clock speedup — the saving is memory; the backward pass through the frozen network is unchanged.

questions.answer_source:
**Use LoRA when:** (1) The base model is large (7B+) and full fine-tuning
is memory-prohibitive. (2) You need to serve multiple tasks from one base model.
(3) The downstream task is reasonably close to the pre-training distribution.
(4) You need fast iteration (LoRA's dominant saving is **memory**—far
smaller optimizer states enable larger batches on the same hardware; the
wall-clock speedup itself is a more modest $\sim$1.2–1.5$\times$, since
activations and the full backward pass through the frozen network remain).

**Use full fine-tuning when:** (1) Maximum quality is required and you have
the compute budget. (2) The domain shift is extreme (e.g., pre-trained on English
web text, fine-tuning for specialized medical code in another language). (3) The
model is small enough that full fine-tuning is feasible (under 1B parameters).
(4) You are doing continued pre-training (not just task adaptation).

**LoRA fails when:** (1) The required weight update is genuinely high-rank—
this happens when the target distribution differs substantially from pre-training
(the model needs to "unlearn" and "relearn" many patterns). (2) The task requires
modifying the embedding layer significantly (e.g., adding a new language). (3) Very
low rank is used for a complex task—the bottleneck starves the model of capacity.

**Where the mechanics live:** rank and $\alpha$ selection, which modules to
target, merging, and QLoRA's internals are canonical in [DL~16]. This question
is the budget-and-data decision, not the knobs—an answer that opens with the
LoRA formula and never reaches "how much data, how much GPU, how many tasks on
one base" has missed what is being asked.

questions.question: What is catastrophic forgetting? How do you mitigate it during fine-tuning?
questions.answer_source:
Catastrophic forgetting occurs when fine-tuning on a downstream task causes the model
to lose knowledge acquired during pre-training. The parameters shift to optimize
the new loss, destructively overwriting representations that encoded general
language understanding. The smaller the fine-tuning dataset and the higher the
learning rate, the more severe the forgetting.

Mitigations: (1)~**Low learning rate** ($1\text{e-}5$ to $5\text{e-}5$)—the
single most important factor. (2)~**Gradual unfreezing** (ULMFiT)—train the
task head first, then unfreeze layers top-to-bottom. (3)~**Regularization**—
weight decay keeps parameters near pre-trained values; EWC penalizes changes to
parameters important for pre-training. (4)~**Early stopping**—fine-tuning
peaks in 2–3 epochs. (5)~**Data replay**—mix pre-training-style data into
fine-tuning batches. (6)~**PEFT methods** (LoRA, adapters)—by only modifying
a small fraction of parameters, the vast majority of pre-trained knowledge is
preserved by design.

PEFT methods are arguably the most effective mitigation because they structurally
prevent forgetting: the base weights are literally frozen.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Cannot define catastrophic forgetting
 
- Only mentions "use a small learning rate" with no other mitigations
 
- Does not connect PEFT methods to forgetting prevention
questions.followups_source:
What is Elastic Weight Consolidation? How does forgetting differ for
encoder-only vs.\ decoder-only models? Can you recover from forgetting?
questions.say:
Catastrophic forgetting is when fine-tuning on a downstream task overwrites what the model learned in pre-training — the parameters move to minimize the new loss and destroy the representations that encoded general language understanding. It's worst when the fine-tuning set is small and the learning rate is high, because then you're taking large steps on a narrow slice of the distribution.

The single biggest lever is the learning rate: 1e-5 to 5e-5 for fine-tuning a pre-trained model. After that, early stopping — fine-tuning usually peaks in two or three epochs and everything past that is mostly forgetting. Gradual unfreezing, the ULMFiT recipe, trains the task head first and then unfreezes layers top down, so the lower layers holding general features move least. Weight decay keeps parameters near their pre-trained values, and EWC does that selectively by penalizing changes to parameters that mattered for pre-training. Data replay — mixing pre-training-style data into your fine-tuning batches — works and is usually the cheapest thing to try first.

But the structural answer is PEFT. With LoRA or adapters the base weights are literally frozen, so the great majority of pre-trained knowledge is preserved by construction rather than by tuning discipline. That's why it's the default now — though it reduces forgetting rather than eliminating it, since the adapter still sits in the forward path.
numbers: Fine-tuning LR: 1e-5 to 5e-5
Fine-tuning typically peaks in 2–3 epochs
red_flags: Cannot actually define catastrophic forgetting when asked.
"Use a small learning rate" and nothing else.
Not connecting PEFT to forgetting prevention.
followups: What is Elastic Weight Consolidation doing?
Does forgetting differ for encoder-only versus decoder-only models?
Can you recover from forgetting after the fact?

questions.chapter_title: Large Language Models and In-Context Learning
questions.question: Explain scaling laws for LLMs. What does the Chinchilla paper tell us about compute-optimal training?
questions.answer_source:
Scaling laws describe the empirical finding that language model loss follows
a power law with respect to model size $N$, dataset size $D$, and total
compute $C$: $L(N) \propto N^{-\alpha_N}$, $L(D) \propto D^{-\alpha_D}$,
$L(C) \propto C^{-\alpha_C}$. The total compute is approximately
$C \approx 6ND$ (forward + backward pass FLOPs).

The Chinchilla paper (Hoffmann et al., 2022) showed that for a fixed compute
budget, the optimal allocation is to scale model size and data proportionally,
with tokens $\approx 20\times$ parameters. This revealed that GPT-3 (175B
params, 300B tokens) was severely undertrained—Chinchilla (70B params, 1.4T
tokens) matched it with far fewer parameters. In practice, most production
models are **over-trained** beyond the Chinchilla ratio (e.g., LLaMA-3 8B
trained on 15T tokens, which is $\sim$94$\times$ the Chinchilla-optimal) to
reduce inference cost—you pay the extra training cost once, but enjoy a
smaller, cheaper model for all future queries.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Stating the Chinchilla ratio as a rigid rule without understanding
 the over-training rationale.

- Not knowing the $C \approx 6ND$ relationship.

- Confusing compute-optimal (minimizes loss for fixed FLOPs) with
 inference-optimal (minimizes serving cost).

- Hand-waving about "bigger models are better" without quantitative
 reasoning.
questions.followups_source:
How do you estimate the total FLOPs for training a model? What
happens when you run out of high-quality data? How do scaling laws change
for fine-tuning vs.\ pretraining?
questions.say:
Scaling laws are the empirical finding that language model loss falls as a power law in model size, dataset size and compute - no plateau in the ranges anyone has measured, and predictable enough that you fit the curve at small scale and extrapolate a run you haven't done yet. The bridge from a budget to a model is that training compute is about six N D: roughly six FLOPs per parameter per token, forward and backward.

Chinchilla showed that for a fixed compute budget people were allocating it wrong. The optimum scales parameters and tokens together, roughly twenty tokens per parameter. GPT-3, at 175 billion parameters on 300 billion tokens, was badly undertrained; Chinchilla at 70 billion on 1.4 trillion matched it with a fraction of the parameters.

Then the part where people get stuck: almost nobody trains Chinchilla-optimal anymore, and that's deliberate. Chinchilla minimizes loss for a fixed training budget and ignores inference entirely. If you're going to serve a model billions of times you want the smallest model that clears your quality bar, so you overtrain hard - Llama 3 8B on 15 trillion tokens is roughly ninety times the Chinchilla-optimal ratio. You pay the training cost once and collect cheaper serving forever.
numbers: Training compute C ~ 6ND FLOPs
Chinchilla: ~20 tokens per parameter
Llama 3 8B: 15T tokens, ~94x the Chinchilla-optimal token ratio
red_flags: Quotes 20:1 as a rule to obey rather than a compute-optimal point that ignores inference cost.
Doesn't know C ~ 6ND, so can't turn a compute budget into a model size.
Confuses compute-optimal with inference-optimal.
followups: Estimate the FLOPs to train a 70B model on 2T tokens.
What happens when you run out of high-quality data?
Do scaling laws look the same for fine-tuning?

questions.chapter_title: Large Language Models and In-Context Learning
questions.question: Why does chain-of-thought prompting improve reasoning? What are its limitations?
questions.say:
Chain-of-thought works because the generated tokens are computation, not just output. A single forward pass gives the model a fixed amount of compute per token; letting it write intermediate steps lets it spend more passes on a hard problem and carry state in the text itself.

Three mechanisms, concretely. Decomposition: a multi-step problem becomes several steps, each of which is inside what the model can do in one shot. Working memory: the reasoning tokens act as an external scratchpad, so the model does not have to hold everything in its hidden state. And distributional shift - pretraining data is full of worked step-by-step explanations, textbooks and tutorials and StackOverflow answers, so prompting for reasoning activates a mode the model already learned rather than teaching it something new.

The limitations matter as much. It costs tokens, so latency and spend go up on every request. The chain can be unfaithful - the model produces reasoning that sounds right and lands on the wrong answer, or bad reasoning and the right answer anyway - which means you cannot treat the chain as an explanation of what the model actually did. It does not help on tasks with no sequential structure, like sentiment or NER, and can hurt by adding noise. And it needs scale: small models produce incoherent chains and get worse, not better.
red_flags: "It makes the model think" with no mechanism.
Not raising unfaithfulness - treating the chain as a true explanation of the model's computation.
Claiming CoT always helps, including on simple or non-sequential tasks.
followups: What is self-consistency and why does it help?
How does zero-shot CoT work?
When does CoT actively hurt?
questions.answer_source:
Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting includes intermediate reasoning steps in
the prompt demonstrations, encouraging the model to decompose complex
problems into smaller sub-steps before producing a final answer. It
improves reasoning for three reasons: (1)~**Decomposition**—complex
multi-step problems are broken into manageable pieces, each within the
model's per-step capability. (2)~**Working memory**—the generated
reasoning tokens act as an external scratchpad, extending the model's
effective working memory beyond what a single forward pass can represent
in its hidden state. (3)~**Distributional shift**—the pretraining
data contains many examples of step-by-step reasoning (textbooks, tutorials,
StackOverflow explanations), so CoT prompting activates a mode the model has
already learned.

Limitations: CoT significantly increases token usage (higher cost and
latency). The reasoning chain can be **unfaithful**—the model may
generate plausible-sounding but incorrect reasoning that happens to reach
the right answer, or correct-looking reasoning that leads to a wrong answer.
It is less effective for tasks that do not involve sequential logic (e.g.,
sentiment analysis, NER). It requires sufficient model scale—smaller models
produce incoherent chains.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Saying "it works because it makes the model think" without explaining
 the mechanism (decomposition, working memory).

- Not mentioning unfaithful reasoning as a limitation.

- Claiming CoT always helps (it can hurt on simple tasks by adding noise).
questions.followups_source:
What is self-consistency and how does it improve on CoT? Can
you explain zero-shot CoT? When would CoT actually hurt performance?

questions.chapter_title: Large Language Models and In-Context Learning
questions.question: Explain in-context learning. Why can models learn from examples in the prompt without gradient updates?
questions.say:
In-context learning is a model doing a task from demonstrations in the prompt with no weight updates, and the honest answer is that we have three partial explanations rather than one settled one.

The cleanest is mechanistic: induction heads. Olsson and colleagues identified a two-head circuit — one head that carries information about the previous token, and one that looks back for an earlier occurrence of the current token and copies whatever followed it. That gives you "A was followed by B earlier, so predict B again," which is literally pattern completion, and the circuit forms during training.

The second framing is Bayesian: pretraining leaves the model with a prior over tasks, and the demonstrations don't teach a new mapping so much as identify which task it already knows. The third is distributional — the pretraining corpus is full of implicit input-output pairs, Q&A threads, translation pairs, docstrings next to code — so continuing such a pattern is exactly what next-token prediction rewarded.

There's also work arguing that attention during in-context learning produces something resembling a gradient step on the demonstrations — implicit fine-tuning inside the forward pass. I'd cite it but flag that it's derived under linear-attention simplifications and how far it carries to real softmax attention is contested.

Practically: format consistency matters most, example selection and ordering matter, and even random labels partly work — which tells you the demonstrations mostly specify the task and the input distribution rather than the label mapping.
red_flags: "It just learns from the examples" with no mechanism
Saying the model memorizes or updates on the examples — no parameters change
Not knowing induction heads or any mechanistic account, and not noting that ICL needs scale
followups: Why do random labels still partly work?
How does ICL performance scale with model size?
How would you select and order demonstrations in practice?
questions.answer_source:
In-context learning (ICL) is the ability of large language models to perform
a task based on demonstrations provided in the prompt, with no parameter
updates. Three complementary hypotheses explain why it works:

(1)~**Implicit Bayesian inference:** The model has learned a prior over
"tasks" during pretraining. The demonstrations update this implicit prior,
allowing the model to identify the task and generate appropriate outputs.

(2)~**Induction heads** (mechanistic explanation): Olsson et al.\ (2022)
identified specific attention circuits—a previous-token head that propagates
positional information and a pattern-matching head that finds earlier
occurrences of a pattern and copies what followed. This two-head circuit
implements "if $A$ followed by $B$ before, then $A$ should be followed by $B$
again."

(3)~**Task recognition:** The internet contains countless implicit
input-output patterns (Q&A forums, translation pairs, code comments).
During pretraining, the model learns to recognize and continue these
patterns. ICL demonstrations activate the appropriate "task mode."

Dai et al.\ (2023) proposed a duality in which transformer attention during
ICL produces updates resembling a single gradient descent step on the
demonstrations—suggesting ICL acts like **implicit fine-tuning**
within the forward pass. The equivalence is derived under linear-attention
simplifications, however, and how well it describes real softmax-attention
transformers is contested.

Key practical factors: example selection (similar examples help), ordering
(recency bias exists), format consistency (critical), and—surprisingly—even
random labels partially work because the model uses format and input
distribution for task inference beyond just label mapping.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Saying "the model just learns from the examples" without explaining
 the mechanism.

- Not knowing about induction heads or any mechanistic explanation.

- Claiming the model "memorizes" the examples (it does not update
 parameters).

- Not mentioning that ICL requires sufficient model scale.
questions.followups_source:
Why do even random labels partially work for ICL? What are
induction heads and how do they enable ICL? How does ICL performance scale
with model size?

questions.chapter_title: Large Language Models and In-Context Learning
questions.question:
Compare few-shot prompting, fine-tuning, and RAG for adapting
an LLM to a new task or domain. When would you use each?
questions.say:
It comes down to three things: how much labeled data you have, how often the knowledge changes, and what your per-query cost budget is.

Few-shot prompting when you have under about fifty examples, the task is well-specified, or it changes frequently. No training, no infrastructure, you iterate in minutes. You pay at inference — long prompts on every call — and it gets inconsistent on genuinely complex tasks while eating context you might want for something else.

Fine-tuning, full or LoRA, when you have a thousand-plus labeled examples and the task is stable. You get consistency, and you often get cheaper inference, because a fine-tuned small model with a short prompt beats a large model carrying a huge few-shot prompt on cost per call. The price is training infrastructure, catastrophic-forgetting risk, and a retraining treadmill as your data drifts.

RAG when the knowledge changes faster than you can retrain, when you need grounding or citations, or when the corpus is simply too large to put in weights. It's the right answer whenever being factually current matters. The catch is that retrieval quality caps everything downstream — a bad retriever gives you a confidently wrong answer with a citation attached — and you now own an index and its freshness pipeline.

In practice they compose, and I'd say so rather than picking one. Fine-tune for format and behavior, RAG for facts, few-shot for the last mile. That's the standard production shape.
red_flags: Recommending one approach without the tradeoffs.
Not mentioning that they compose — fine-tune for behavior, retrieve for facts.
Ignoring per-query cost and latency, which is often what actually decides it.
followups: When would you combine fine-tuning with RAG?
What do you do in a domain with zero labeled data?
How would you evaluate which strategy is winning?
questions.answer_source:
These three approaches form a spectrum of adaptation strategies:

**Few-shot prompting:** Provide examples in the context window. No
training required. Best when: you have a capable model, the task is
well-defined, you have very few labeled examples ($<$50), or the task changes
frequently. Limitations: constrained by context window, inconsistent for
complex tasks, expensive per query (long prompts).

**Fine-tuning (full or LoRA):** Update model parameters on
task-specific data. Best when: you have $>$1000 labeled examples, the task
is stable (not changing daily), you need high accuracy and consistency,
or you need to reduce inference cost (a fine-tuned small model replaces a
large model with long prompts). Limitations: requires training
infrastructure, risk of catastrophic forgetting, needs ongoing maintenance
as data evolves.

**RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation):** Retrieve relevant documents
at inference time and include them in the prompt. Best when: the knowledge
base changes frequently, you need grounding and citations, the domain
knowledge does not fit in model weights (too large or too dynamic), or
factual accuracy is critical and hallucination must be minimized.
Limitations: retrieval quality caps generation quality, adds latency, requires
maintaining a retrieval index.

In practice, these are often combined: a fine-tuned model with RAG for
up-to-date knowledge, or few-shot prompting with retrieved examples. The
decision framework is: how much data do you have, how often does the task
or knowledge change, what are your latency and cost constraints, and how
critical is factual grounding?
questions.red_flags_source:
- Recommending only one approach without discussing tradeoffs.

- Not mentioning that these can be combined.

- Ignoring cost and latency considerations.

- Saying "just use fine-tuning" without considering data requirements
 and maintenance burden.

- Saying "just use RAG" without considering retrieval quality
 limitations.
questions.followups_source:
When would you combine fine-tuning with RAG? How do you handle
a domain where you have zero labeled data? How would you evaluate which
adaptation strategy works best?

questions.chapter_title: Large Language Models and In-Context Learning
questions.question: How does an LLM actually call a tool? Walk me through the full round trip from tool definition to final answer.
questions.answer_source:
The round trip has five stages. (1)~**Schema in context:** each tool
is declared as a JSON-Schema definition (name, description, typed
parameters), serialized into the model's context by its chat template.
(2)~**Constrained generation of a call:** the model—trained via SFT
on tool-use trajectories to emit calls in its template's format—produces
a structured block (tool `name` + JSON arguments) instead of prose
and halts with a distinguished stop reason (e.g.,
`stop_reason = tool_use`); serving stacks additionally apply
constrained decoding against the schema, so the emitted call is guaranteed
syntactically valid. (3)~**Execution by the caller:** the application
receives the call, validates the arguments, and runs the function. The
model never executes anything—it only emits text describing what it
wants run. (4)~**Observation:** the result—or an error, flagged as
such—is appended to the conversation as a tool-result message tied to
the call's ID. (5)~**Continuation:** the model reads the observation
and either answers the user or issues further calls; an agent loop is this
cycle iterated.

Two format-level details signal depth: **parallel tool calls**
(several independent calls in one assistant turn, executed concurrently to
save round trips) and **tool-choice forcing** (`auto` /
required / named tool / none)—forcing a named tool whose input schema is
your desired output schema is how structured-output extraction is
implemented in practice. Finally, constrained decoding guarantees only
**syntax**; choosing the right tool with the right argument values is a
model-quality problem no grammar can fix.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Saying or implying that **the model executes the function**.
 The model emits a request; the application executes it and returns an
 observation.

- Treating function calling as pure prompting—not knowing it is
 trained in via SFT on trajectories with special tokens and formats.

- Believing constrained decoding makes tool use "correct" (it
 guarantees valid syntax, not correct tool selection or argument values).

- Not knowing that tool errors are returned to the model as
 observations for it to react to—proposing instead that the application
 silently retries or crashes.

- No awareness of chat-template mismatch as a failure mode when
 self-hosting open-weight models.
questions.followups_source:
How would you get reliable structured JSON out of a model with
no tool involved at all? What breaks if your serving stack renders tools
in a different format than the model was trained on? How do you cap cost
when a model gets stuck re-calling a failing tool?
questions.say:
Five stages, and the thing to get right up front is that the model never executes anything.

First, the tool definitions go into the context: each one a JSON-Schema block with a name, a description and typed parameters, serialized by the model's chat template. Second, the model emits a call instead of prose. It's been fine-tuned on tool-use trajectories to produce a structured block — tool name plus JSON arguments — and it halts with a distinguished stop reason, tool_use rather than end_turn. Serving stacks typically layer constrained decoding against the schema on top, so the call is guaranteed to parse.

Third, the application executes: it receives the call, validates the arguments, runs the function. This is the step candidates get wrong — the model only emits text describing what it wants run. Fourth, the observation goes back, appended as a tool-result message keyed to that call's ID — the result, or the error explicitly flagged as an error. Fifth, the model reads it and either answers or issues more calls. An agent loop is just this cycle iterated.

Two details that signal depth: parallel tool calls, several independent calls in one turn executed concurrently to save round trips; and tool-choice forcing — auto, required, a named tool, or none. Forcing a named tool whose input schema is your desired output schema is how structured extraction is actually implemented. And constrained decoding only guarantees syntax; picking the right tool with the right arguments is a model-quality problem no grammar fixes.
red_flags: Saying or implying the model executes the function — it emits a request, the application runs it.
Treating tool use as pure prompting, with no awareness it's trained in via SFT on trajectories and special formats.
Believing constrained decoding makes tool use correct — it guarantees syntax, not tool or argument choice.
Not knowing tool errors go back to the model as observations rather than being swallowed or retried silently.
followups: How would you get reliable structured JSON with no tool involved at all?
What breaks if your serving stack renders tools in a different format than the model was trained on?
How do you cap cost when a model gets stuck re-calling a failing tool?

questions.question: Walk me through the RLHF pipeline step by step. What are the three stages?
questions.answer_source:
The RLHF pipeline has three stages.

**Stage 1—SFT:** Fine-tune the pretrained model on high-quality
demonstration data (instruction-response pairs) to teach it the format and
style of helpful responses. This produces the SFT model, which also serves
as the reference policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ for subsequent stages.

**Stage 2—Reward Model Training:** Collect human preferences: for
each prompt, generate two (or more) responses, and have annotators indicate
which is better. Train a reward model using the Bradley-Terry framework:
$\loss_{\text{RM}} = -\E[\log \sigma(r(x, y_w) - r(x, y_l))]$.
The RM shares the base model architecture but replaces the LM head with a
scalar output.

**Stage 3—RL Optimization (PPO):** Optimize the policy to maximize
$\E[r(x, y)] - \beta \cdot \KL(\pi_\theta \| \pi_{\text{ref}})$. PPO
uses a clipped surrogate objective for stable updates. The KL penalty
prevents reward hacking by keeping the policy close to the SFT model.
This stage requires four models in memory: policy, reference, reward model,
and value function (critic).
questions.red_flags_source:
- Cannot name all three stages or gets the order wrong.

- Skips the reward model and jumps from SFT to RL.

- Does not mention the KL penalty or its purpose.

- Confuses the reward model with the value function.
questions.followups_source:
How many models do you need in GPU memory during PPO? What
happens if the reward model is poor? Why is the SFT model used as the
reference rather than the pretrained model?
questions.say:
Three stages: supervised fine-tuning, then a reward model, then RL against that reward.

SFT first. You fine-tune the pretrained base on high-quality demonstration data, instruction and response pairs, so the model learns the format and register of a helpful answer. That checkpoint does double duty - it's the starting policy, and it becomes the reference the KL penalty is measured against later.

Stage two, the reward model. For each prompt you sample two or more responses and have annotators say which is better, then train under Bradley-Terry - a logistic loss on the difference in scores between preferred and dispreferred - so the model only ever learns relative quality, never an absolute scale. Architecturally it's the same base model with the language modeling head swapped for a scalar head.

Stage three, PPO. Optimize the policy to maximize expected reward minus beta times the KL from the reference. The KL term is not optional: without it the policy walks off into whatever degenerate text the reward model happens to score highly, which is reward hacking.

The practical detail interviewers like: stage three holds four models in memory at once - policy, frozen reference, reward model, and the value function critic. That footprint is a big part of why DPO got popular.
numbers: PPO stage holds 4 models in memory: policy, reference, reward model, critic
red_flags: Gets the order wrong, or jumps from SFT straight to RL with no reward model.
Doesn't mention the KL penalty, or can't say what it prevents.
Confuses the reward model with the value function; different models, different jobs.
followups: How many models are resident during PPO?
What happens if the reward model is weak?
Why is the SFT model the reference rather than the pretrained base?

questions.question: What is reward hacking? How does the KL penalty help? When does it fail?
questions.say:
Reward hacking is the policy learning to exploit the reward model instead of actually getting better. The reward model is a proxy trained on finite preference data, so it has blind spots, and PPO will find them, because finding the argmax of the reward is exactly what it is optimising. The concrete forms you see are verbosity, where the RM prefers longer answers so the policy pads; sycophancy, where it agrees with whatever the user asserted; and impressive-looking formatting with nothing inside it.

The KL penalty against the reference policy is the main defence, and the logic is distributional. The reward model was trained on completions from the SFT model or something close to it, so its scores are trustworthy near that distribution and increasingly unreliable as you move away. Penalising KL keeps the policy inside the region where the proxy still tracks the thing you actually care about.

It fails in three ways. If the reward model's bias is systematic rather than a narrow quirk - it just likes long responses everywhere - the policy can hack it without leaving the KL ball at all, because the hack is available nearby. If beta is set too low you have bought nothing. And the penalty anchors you to the reference model, so anything wrong with the SFT model is something the KL term actively preserves.
red_flags: Defining reward hacking loosely as "the model gets things wrong".
Not connecting the KL penalty to where the reward model's scores are actually reliable.
Claiming the KL penalty solves reward hacking.
followups: What does the over-optimisation curve look like?
How would you detect reward hacking in production?
How do reward-model ensembles help?
questions.answer_source:
Reward hacking occurs when the policy exploits imperfections in the reward
model rather than genuinely improving response quality. The RM is a
proxy for human preferences trained on finite data, so it inevitably has
blind spots. Common examples: the RM gives higher scores to longer
responses (verbosity hack), sycophantic agreement, or responses with
impressive-sounding but vacuous formatting.

The KL penalty $\beta \cdot \KL(\pi_\theta \| \pi_{\text{ref}})$ is the
primary defense. It constrains the policy to stay close to the SFT model,
limiting how far it can drift into regions where the RM's predictions are
unreliable. Intuitively, the RM was trained on outputs from $\pi_{\text{ref}}$
(or similar), so its predictions are most trustworthy near that distribution.

The KL penalty fails when: (1)~the reward model has **systematic** biases
(e.g., always preferring longer responses)—the policy can hack these
biases even within the KL budget; (2)~$\beta$ is set too low, giving the
policy too much room to diverge; (3)~the reference model itself has
problematic behaviors that the KL penalty preserves.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Defines reward hacking vaguely as "the model being wrong."

- Does not connect the KL penalty to the RM's distribution shift.

- Claims the KL penalty fully solves reward hacking.

- Cannot give concrete examples of reward hacking.
questions.followups_source:
What is the over-optimization curve? How would you detect
reward hacking in practice? How do RM ensembles help? Design a reward
for a coding agent that resists test-hacking
(Section~: hidden and property-based tests,
a hardened read-only sandbox, transcript audits).

questions.question: Explain DPO. How does it relate to RLHF, and what are its limitations?
questions.say:
DPO turns RLHF into a single supervised loss by noticing that the reward model never had to be a separate artifact. The KL-constrained objective RLHF optimizes has a closed-form optimum: the optimal policy is the reference policy reweighted by the exponentiated reward. Invert that and the reward is beta times the log ratio of policy to reference, plus a term that depends only on the prompt. Substitute it into the Bradley-Terry preference model and that prompt term cancels, because you're comparing two responses to the same prompt. What's left is a loss on the policy itself — push up the log ratio on the chosen response, push it down on the rejected one, with a sigmoid so the gradient fades once you're comfortably winning the pair.

The practical win is fewer moving parts: two models instead of four, no reward model, no rollouts, no PPO. It trains like ordinary supervised learning, so it's far more stable and much cheaper.

The limitations are real. It's offline — you optimize against a fixed preference set with no exploration, so it can't discover responses better than what's in the data. There's no explicit reward model left, which you'd want for monitoring, for best-of-n sampling, or for reranking at inference. And it's sensitive to the reference policy: DPO from a poorly supervised-fine-tuned reference inherits that weakness.
red_flags: Can't say where the prompt-dependent term cancels
Presenting DPO as just another RLHF variant, with no link to the KL-constrained optimum
Claiming DPO strictly dominates RLHF; not mentioning that it's offline
followups: What is the implicit reward in DPO?
When would you still run full RLHF?
What does beta control in practice?
questions.whiteboard: $r(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}+C(x)$ — write this single line and say: the reward is implicit in the policy, and when you put it into Bradley-Terry the $C(x)$ cancels in the difference between chosen and rejected. That cancellation is the whole trick.
questions.answer_source:
DPO reformulates RLHF as a supervised learning problem. The key insight
is that the optimal policy under the KL-constrained RM maximization
objective has a closed form:
$\pi^*(y|x) \propto \pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x) \exp(r(x,y)/\beta)$. Rearranging,
the reward is a function of the policy:
$r(x,y) = \beta \log(\pi^*(y|x)/\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)) + C(x)$.
Substituting this into the Bradley-Terry model, the prompt-dependent
constant $C(x)$ cancels in the reward **difference**, yielding the DPO
loss:
$\loss_{\text{DPO}} = -\E[\log \sigma(\beta(\log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w|x)} - \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l|x)}))]$.

This directly optimizes the policy on preference data without a separate
reward model or RL algorithm. Advantages: simpler (2 models vs.\ 4),
more stable training (standard supervised loss), lower compute.
Limitations: no explicit reward for monitoring or best-of-$n$ sampling,
offline (no exploration during training), and reference model quality
is critical.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Cannot sketch the derivation or explain where the partition
 function cancels.

- Treats DPO as "just an alternative to RLHF" without understanding
 the mathematical connection.

- Claims DPO is always better than RLHF.

- Does not mention the offline limitation.
questions.followups_source:
Derive the DPO loss from the RLHF objective. What is the
implicit reward in DPO? When would you prefer RLHF over DPO?

questions.question:
Compare BM25 vs.\ dense retrieval. When would you use each? When
would you combine them?
questions.say:
In production, almost always both — they fail in complementary ways, which is the whole argument.

BM25 is lexical: an inverted index scoring documents on query-term overlap with TF-IDF-style weighting. No training data, extremely fast, interpretable, and unbeatable on exact strings — entity names, part numbers, error codes, legal citations. Its failure is vocabulary mismatch: search "automobile" and miss the document that says "car."

Dense retrieval embeds queries and documents into a shared space with trained encoders and does nearest-neighbor search. It handles paraphrase and conceptual queries, which is precisely BM25's blind spot. Its failures are the mirror image: it can miss a rare exact token entirely, it needs training data and GPU infrastructure, and when it's wrong you can't tell why.

So BM25 alone when you have no training data or the domain is precise-terminology-heavy — medical codes, statutes, SKUs. Dense alone when queries and documents genuinely use different vocabulary and you have data to train on. But the honest production answer is hybrid, fused with reciprocal rank fusion, and it consistently beats either leg because the errors don't correlate.

The thing I'd add is the cost of that: hybrid doubles your operational surface — two indexes, two freshness pipelines, two things that page you. So I'd want per-slice evaluation showing where each leg actually earns its keep, rather than a global average that says hybrid is better and tells you nothing about which queries need it.
red_flags: Calling BM25 obsolete or legacy-only.
Can't explain the vocabulary mismatch problem concretely.
Never mentioning hybrid — or mentioning it without acknowledging the cost of running two indexes.
followups: What is SPLADE and how does it bridge sparse and dense?
How would you choose the RRF constant?
If you had to drop one leg, which and why?
questions.answer_source:
**BM25** uses lexical matching via an inverted index: it scores documents
based on query term overlap, weighted by TF-IDF-like statistics. Strengths:
handles exact terms (entity names, product IDs, error codes), no training data
needed, extremely fast, interpretable. Weakness: no semantic understanding—
fails on vocabulary mismatch ("automobile" vs.\ "car").

**Dense retrieval** (bi-encoder) embeds queries and documents in a shared
vector space using trained neural encoders. Strengths: captures semantic
similarity, handles paraphrases and conceptual queries. Weakness: may miss
exact lexical matches, requires training data and GPU infrastructure, less
interpretable.

**When to use BM25:** low-resource settings (no training data), domains
with precise terminology (medical codes, legal statutes), when exact matching
is critical. **When to use dense:** semantic search, FAQ matching, when
queries and documents use different vocabulary. **Combine them:** almost
always in production. Hybrid retrieval with RRF consistently outperforms
either alone because their failure modes are complementary. BM25 catches
what dense misses (rare terms) and vice versa. If the interviewer pushes past
this into the engines themselves—BM25 parameter tuning and inverted-index
serving, or the fusion arithmetic and how the two legs are trained—that is
[SR 2] and [SR 4]. What the RAG answer owes is the routing judgment above,
plus the acknowledgement that hybrid doubles the operational surface (two
indexes, two freshness pipelines) and therefore needs per-slice evaluation.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Says BM25 is "obsolete" or "only for legacy systems"
 
- Cannot explain the vocabulary mismatch problem
 
- Does not mention the option to combine them
 
- Cannot articulate when BM25 would outperform dense retrieval
questions.followups_source:
What is SPLADE and how does it bridge sparse and dense? How would
you decide the RRF constant $k$? What is the BEIR benchmark and why does it
matter for retrieval?

questions.question: How would you evaluate a RAG system end-to-end? What metrics would you track?
questions.answer_source:
RAG evaluation must be decomposed into three layers. **Layer 1:
Retrieval quality.** Metrics: Recall@$K$ (most important—if the relevant
chunk is not retrieved, the LLM cannot use it), MRR, NDCG@$K$. Requires a
labeled set of (query, relevant chunk) pairs.

**Layer 2: Generation quality.** Given retrieved context, does the model
produce a good answer? Metrics: answer relevancy, completeness, and coherence.
Measured via human evaluation or LLM-as-judge.

**Layer 3: Faithfulness.** The RAG-specific critical metric: does the
answer contain **only** information supported by the retrieved context?
Measured via NLI-based verification, LLM-as-judge faithfulness scoring, or
citation verification. Frameworks like RAGAS compute these metrics
automatically.

**End-to-end:** answer correctness (is the final answer factually
correct?) and user satisfaction (thumbs up/down, CSAT scores).

Key insight: when the system produces a wrong answer, you must diagnose
**which layer** failed. Retrieval failure needs better embeddings or hybrid
search; ranking failure needs re-ranking; generation failure needs better
prompting or model.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Evaluates only the final answer without decomposing into layers
 
- Does not mention faithfulness as a metric
 
- Cannot name specific metrics (Recall@$K$, NDCG, MRR)
 
- "We'll just use human evaluation" without a concrete plan
questions.followups_source:
How would you build a labeled evaluation set for RAG? What are
the biases of LLM-as-judge evaluation? How do you detect quality regression
in production?
questions.say:
You have to decompose it, because a single end-to-end score tells you nothing about what to fix. Three layers plus an end-to-end number.

Retrieval first, and recall@k is the one that matters most — if the right chunk isn't in the context, nothing downstream can save you, so it's a hard ceiling on the whole system. NDCG and MRR on top of that when ordering matters, since position in the context window affects how much the model uses a chunk. This needs a labeled set of query-to-relevant-chunk pairs, and building that honestly is the real work.

Generation second: given the context that was actually retrieved, is the answer relevant, complete and coherent? That's human evaluation or LLM-as-judge. Third, and this is the RAG-specific one, faithfulness: does the answer contain only what the retrieved context supports? You measure it with NLI-style entailment checks against the retrieved chunks, LLM-as-judge faithfulness scoring, or citation verification where every claim has to map to a cited span. RAGAS computes versions of these automatically. Then end-to-end answer correctness against a gold set, plus production signals — thumbs up and down, CSAT.

The reason to keep the layers separate is triage. Wrong answer with the right chunk retrieved is a generation or prompting problem. Wrong answer with the chunk missing entirely is an embedding or hybrid-search problem. Chunk retrieved but ranked twentieth is a reranking problem. Different fixes, and a blended score can't tell you which one you have.
red_flags: Scoring only the final answer, with no decomposition into retrieval, generation and faithfulness.
Never mentioning faithfulness — the metric that's specific to RAG.
"We'll just use human evaluation" with no concrete plan or labeled set.
followups: How would you build the labeled evaluation set?
What are the biases of LLM-as-judge?
How do you detect a quality regression in production?

questions.question: When should you use RAG vs. fine-tuning vs. long context?
questions.answer_source:
These serve different purposes and are not mutually exclusive.

**RAG:** when knowledge changes frequently, when you need attribution and
citations, when the knowledge base is too large for any context window, and when
verifiability matters (legal, medical, compliance). RAG's knowledge can be
updated by re-indexing without retraining.

**Fine-tuning:** when you need to change the model's **behavior**—
its tone, format, instruction-following style, or domain reasoning patterns.
Fine-tuning encodes knowledge into weights, so it cannot be easily updated
and provides no attribution. Best for: style adaptation, domain-specific
instruction following, distillation.

**Long context:** when the corpus is small enough to fit in a context
window, when you need real-time document analysis ("summarize this PDF"),
or when pipeline simplicity is paramount. Limitations: cost scales linearly
with context length, "lost in the middle" problem, context window is still
finite.

**Combine:** fine-tune + RAG is the most common production pattern
(fine-tune for domain behavior, RAG for knowledge grounding). Long context
+ RAG is emerging: retrieve a larger set and let the model process everything.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Treats these as mutually exclusive
 
- Says "just use RAG for everything" or "just fine-tune"
 
- Cannot articulate when fine-tuning beats RAG (behavior vs.\ knowledge)
 
- Ignores cost, latency, and updateability considerations
questions.followups_source:
What is RAFT (Retrieval Augmented Fine-Tuning)? How do the
tradeoffs change as context windows grow to 1M+ tokens? When would you
fine-tune the retrieval model vs.\ the generation model?
questions.say:
They solve different problems, so the question is which one you need, and usually the answer is more than one. The clean split: RAG is for knowledge, fine-tuning is for behavior, long context is for a document you have in hand right now.

RAG when the knowledge changes, when you need citations, when the corpus is far too big for any context window, or when someone has to audit why the model said what it said - legal, medical, compliance. Its real advantage is that you update it by re-indexing, with no training run at all.

Fine-tuning when you want to change how the model behaves rather than what it knows: tone, output format, instruction-following style, domain reasoning patterns, or distilling a big model into a small one. Knowledge baked into weights can't be updated cheaply and carries no attribution, which is why using fine-tuning as a knowledge store disappoints.

Long context when the corpus fits, when the task genuinely is "analyze this PDF," or when pipeline simplicity beats efficiency. The limits are that cost scales with context length on every call, retrieval inside a long context degrades in the middle, and the window is still finite.

In production it's usually fine-tune for behavior plus RAG for knowledge.
red_flags: Treats them as three competing options rather than complementary layers.
Can't articulate the behavior-versus-knowledge line, so recommends fine-tuning to teach facts.
Ignores update cadence, per-call cost, and attribution requirements.
followups: What is RAFT, retrieval-augmented fine-tuning?
How do the trade-offs change at million-token context windows?
Would you fine-tune the retriever or the generator?

questions.question: Explain the bi-encoder versus cross-encoder tradeoff in retrieval. How would you use both in a production system?
questions.say:
Bi-encoders are cheap and shallow, cross-encoders are expensive and deep, and in production you use both in a funnel.

A bi-encoder encodes query and document independently into vectors and scores with a dot product. Because the documents are encoded offline and sit in an ANN index, search is sublinear in corpus size, so you can run it over hundreds of millions of documents. What you give up is any interaction between query and document tokens - the model has to commit to a document representation before it has seen the query.

A cross-encoder concatenates query and document and runs them through the transformer together, so every query token can attend to every document token. That is dramatically better relevance, and it is why it wins every quality comparison. It is also one forward pass per document, so full-corpus search is linear and hopeless past a few hundred or a thousand candidates.

So the standard pattern is two stages: bi-encoder, or hybrid BM25 plus dense, retrieves the top hundred, and a cross-encoder reranks those down to a final five. Reranking a hundred documents costs a couple of hundred milliseconds, which most applications absorb.

The point I would emphasise is the evaluation consequence. Because the expensive model only sees a few candidates, the first stage is judged on recall at its handoff depth, never on precision - if the right answer is not in the hundred, no reranker recovers it.
numbers: Reranking top-100 with a cross-encoder: ~200-500 ms
red_flags: Cannot say why cross-encoders win - no mention of joint encoding or cross-attention.
Proposing a cross-encoder over the whole corpus.
Evaluating the first stage on precision rather than recall at the handoff depth.
followups: Where does ColBERT sit between the two?
How do you decide how many candidates to rerank?
How does cross-encoder to bi-encoder distillation work?
questions.answer_source:
A **bi-encoder** independently encodes query and document into vectors,
then computes similarity via dot product or cosine. Because documents can be
pre-encoded offline and stored in an ANN index, retrieval is $O(\log N)$ over
the corpus. However, no cross-attention means the model cannot perform deep
query-document interaction.

A **cross-encoder** concatenates (query, document) and processes them
jointly through a full transformer with bidirectional attention. This allows
rich token-level interaction (the model can see both query and document tokens
simultaneously), producing much higher quality relevance scores. However,
it requires a forward pass per document, making it $O(N)$ for full-corpus
search—impractical beyond $\sim$1000 candidates.

**In production:** use both in a two-stage pipeline. Stage 1: bi-encoder
(or hybrid BM25 + bi-encoder) retrieves top-100 candidates cheaply. Stage 2:
cross-encoder re-ranks these 100 candidates to select the final top-5. This
gives you the bi-encoder's efficiency at scale with the cross-encoder's
precision for the final selection. The latency overhead of re-ranking 100
documents is $\sim$200–500ms, acceptable for most applications.

**Distillation:** for even better bi-encoder performance, use the
cross-encoder to score a large training set, then train the bi-encoder to
approximate these scores. Choosing the handoff depth from marginal-recall
curves, reranker latency by candidate count and model class, and the
distillation recipes themselves are canonical in [SR 4]; the pipeline-level
claim to defend here is that the expensive model must run on few candidates,
so the first stage is evaluated on recall at its handoff depth, never on
precision.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Cannot explain why cross-encoders are higher quality (no mention
 of cross-attention or joint encoding)
 
- Proposes using a cross-encoder for full-corpus search
 
- Does not mention the two-stage pipeline as the standard pattern
 
- Confuses bi-encoder with cross-encoder architecturally
questions.followups_source:
What is ColBERT and where does it fall in the bi-encoder vs.\
cross-encoder spectrum? How would you decide how many candidates to re-rank?
How does distillation from cross-encoder to bi-encoder work?

questions.question: Your RAG system answers factual lookup questions well but fails on questions that require combining facts across documents — "which customers on the legacy plan have an open P1 ticket?" or "did the Q3 pricing change contradict the renewal terms?" Retrieval looks healthy: every returned chunk is on topic. Diagnose it.
questions.say:
This looks like a reasoning failure but it's an evidence-set failure, and that distinction is the diagnosis. The retriever optimizes chunk-level similarity, so every chunk it returns is individually on topic. Nothing scores whether the set is sufficient to answer. "A relevant chunk was retrieved" and "the answer is in the context" are different claims, and recall@k only checks the first.

There's a structural reason: a composed question embeds to roughly the average of its parts, landing near documents that discuss both topics generically rather than the two chunks that each answer one half. And for a genuine second hop the bridging entity isn't in the query at all, so no single-shot retrieval at any k reaches it.

Confirm it before fixing: annotate a slice of reasoning queries with the complete evidence set and measure all-hops recall — did we get every required chunk — next to ordinary recall@k. The gap is the diagnosis. Then hand the generator the gold chunks; if it answers, the defect is retrieval completeness, and if it doesn't, you have a real synthesis limit.

Fixes cheapest first: query decomposition for independent sub-questions, iterative retrieval with a hop cap when hop two depends on hop one, and retrieval units that match the question — customer records, not paragraphs mentioning one. But "which customers on the legacy plan have an open P1" is a join with a filter; that belongs in SQL, and the mature system routes set-valued queries there.
red_flags: Reaching for a stronger model or prompt tweaks when the facts were never in context
Citing recall@k as proof retrieval is healthy without asking whether the set was sufficient
Never considering that set-valued or aggregate queries belong in a database or knowledge graph
followups: How would you build a multi-hop eval set without hand-annotating every hop?
What termination condition and budget would you give an iterative retrieval loop?
When do you tell the team a query class needs SQL rather than a better retriever?
questions.answer_source:
The symptom looks like a reasoning failure, so the instinct is to blame the
generator. It is almost always an **evidence-set** failure, and the
differential is what separates the two.

**Work the differential first.**
(1)~**Retrieval returns locally relevant chunks, not a sufficient set.**
Each chunk is individually similar to the query, which is exactly what the
retriever optimizes; but the answer lives in facts spread across several
documents, and nothing in the pipeline scores a **set** for sufficiency.
"All $k$ chunks are relevant" and "the $k$ chunks contain the answer" are
different statements, and recall@$K$ measured as "did any relevant chunk
appear" will report the system as healthy while it is not.
(2)~**Chunk-level similarity cannot express a multi-hop query.** A
composed question embeds to roughly the average of its parts, which lands near
documents that discuss both topics generically rather than near the two
specific chunks that each answer one part—and for a genuine second hop the
bridging entity is not in the query at all ("the film that won the Palme d'Or"
must be resolved to a title before the director can be retrieved), so no
single-shot query, at any $k$, can reach it. Aggregation queries are worse
still: "which customers" asks for a set defined by a predicate, and there is
no chunk whose text is that set.
(3)~**The generator cannot synthesize what was never retrieved.** Given a
partial evidence set, a model either hedges or fills the gap from parametric
memory—which is why the failure surfaces as confident, plausible, wrong
prose, and why upgrading the model moves the number very little.

**Confirm it before fixing it.** Build a small labelled slice of
reasoning queries and annotate the **full** evidence set for each—every
chunk needed, not one gold chunk. Then measure all-hops recall (did retrieval
return **all** required chunks?) alongside the usual recall@$K$; the gap
between the two curves is the diagnosis. Confirm with an oracle-context test:
hand the generator the gold chunks and re-ask. If it now answers, the defect
is retrieval completeness; if it still fails, you have a real synthesis limit
and the fixes below will not help. This is the layered decomposition of
Section~ applied to a failure mode that hides between
its layers.

**Fixes, cheapest first.**
(1)~**Query decomposition.** One LLM call before retrieval splits the
question into sub-queries, each retrieved independently, with the union
assembled for synthesis (Section~). This is the right
first move when the parts are **independent**—comparisons, multi-entity
lookups, "and" questions—and it costs one extra call plus $N$ retrievals.
(2)~**Iterative (multi-hop) retrieval.** When hop~2 depends on hop~1's
answer, decomposition cannot help: the loop must retrieve, read, reformulate,
and retrieve again. Budget it explicitly—a hop cap, a termination
condition, and a per-query spend ceiling—because $N$ hops is $N$ retrievals
and $N{+}1$ generations, which turns a 300\,ms query into seconds. The
agentic form, where retrieval is a tool the model may invoke zero or more
times and the loop decides when it has enough, is [DL 27]; what an agent loop
does to the retrieval tier's QPS and tail latency is [SR 8].
(3)~**Higher $K$ with a reranker.** Raising first-stage $K$ so that all
hops sit in the candidate pool, then reranking down to a clean context, is the
cheapest infrastructure change and sometimes enough—but only for queries
whose evidence was reachable by the original query in the first place. It
does nothing for a second hop whose entity is still unknown, and it is not
free: more chunks in context is more distraction and more exposure to
lost-in-the-middle (Section~), which is precisely why the
reranker, not the raw $K$, is the load-bearing part
(Section~).
(4)~**Aggregation-friendly chunking and indexing.** If the question is
about a customer, the retrievable unit should be a customer record, not the
paragraph that happens to mention one. Parent-child retrieval, document-level
summaries indexed alongside chunks, and entity-level or table-level records
give the retriever something whose embedding actually denotes the thing being
asked about (Section~). This is a reindex, so it is a
sprint, not an afternoon.
(5)~**Admit when it is not a RAG query.** "Which customers on the
legacy plan have an open P1 ticket" is a join with a filter over two systems
of record. A text-to-SQL path or a graph traversal answers it exactly, in
milliseconds, with no chance of a missed chunk; no amount of retrieval tuning
will make similarity search do it correctly, because the query is set-valued
and the index is not. The mature answer routes by query class—a light
classifier or planner sends set-valued, aggregate, and comparative queries to
the structured path and keeps lookups on the vector path, with retrieval as
one tool among several. Teams that miss this spend a quarter rebuilding a
worse database out of embeddings.

Finally, hold the reasoning slice out as its own evaluation segment
permanently. Averaged into one headline number it disappears, and every fix
above trades some cost or latency on the factual slice to buy it back.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Jumps to "use a stronger model" or prompt tweaks when the required
 facts were never in the context
 
- Reports recall@$K$ ("a relevant chunk was retrieved") as evidence
 that retrieval is fine, without ever asking whether the set was
 **sufficient**
 
- Raises $k$ with no reranker, adding distractors and lost-in-the-middle
 exposure while leaving dependent hops unreachable
 
- Reaches straight for an agentic multi-hop loop without costing its
 latency and spend
 
- Never considers that set-valued or aggregate queries belong to a
 database or a knowledge graph rather than to RAG
questions.followups_source:
How would you build a labelled evaluation set for multi-hop queries
without hand-annotating every hop? What termination condition would you give
an iterative retrieval loop, and what does one cost per query? At what point
do you tell the team a query class needs a knowledge graph or a SQL layer
rather than a better retriever?

questions.question: What is BLEU? Derive it step by step. What are its limitations?
questions.say:
BLEU scores a machine translation by n-gram precision against one or more references, with two corrections that stop it being trivially gameable.

The first is clipping. For each n-gram in the candidate you count its occurrences but cap that count at the most times it appears in any single reference. Without it you could output "the the the the" and score perfect unigram precision. The second is the brevity penalty. Precision alone rewards being short — a one-word output that happens to match is a hundred percent precise — so if the candidate is shorter than the reference you multiply by an exponential penalty; longer or equal, no penalty.

You compute modified precision for unigrams through 4-grams and combine them with a uniform-weight geometric mean. Geometric matters: if any order scores zero the whole thing is zero, which is why sentence-level BLEU on short sentences is so unstable and why you report corpus-level.

For limitations — it's precision-only, with the brevity penalty as a crude stand-in for recall. No semantic awareness, so a good paraphrase gets punished. Poor correlation with human judgment at the segment level. Biased against morphologically rich languages. And it's capped by the number and quality of your references.

In practice I'd report COMET, which is neural, trained on human judgments and correlates far better — and still report BLEU, because reviewers expect it.
red_flags: "It's n-gram overlap" and nothing more — no clipping, no brevity penalty.
Not knowing why the brevity penalty exists.
Saying BLEU measures recall, or being unable to name a single limitation.
followups: What is SacreBLEU and why did it need to exist?
How does BLEU compare with ROUGE?
How would you evaluate translation into a language like Finnish?
questions.answer_source:
BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) is an automatic metric for evaluating
machine translation quality by measuring n-gram precision between a candidate
translation and one or more reference translations.

**Derivation:**

 
- **Modified n-gram precision $p_n$:** For each n-gram in the
 candidate, count how many times it appears, but clip this count by
 the maximum number of times it appears in any single reference.
 This prevents gaming (e.g., repeating "the" 20 times).
 \[
 p_n = \frac{\sum_{\text{n-gram} \in C}\min(\text{Count}_C,\;\max_R \text{Count}_R)}{\sum_{\text{n-gram} \in C}\text{Count}_C}
 \]

 
- **Geometric mean:** Combine $p_1$ through $p_4$ using a weighted
 geometric mean with uniform weights $w_n = 1/4$:
 $\exp\!\bigl(\sum_{n=1}^{4}\frac{1}{4}\ln p_n\bigr)$.
 This ensures that failure at any n-gram order zeroes the entire score.

 
- **Brevity penalty:**
 $\text{BP} = \exp\!\bigl(\min(0, 1 - |R|/|C|)\bigr)$.
 Penalizes candidates shorter than the reference to prevent trivially
 high precision from short outputs.

 
- **Final score:**
 $\text{BLEU} = \text{BP} \times \exp\!\bigl(\sum_{n=1}^{4}w_n \ln p_n\bigr)$.

**Limitations:**
(1)~Precision-only: no recall component beyond the crude brevity penalty.
(2)~No semantic awareness: valid paraphrases are penalized.
(3)~Poor segment-level correlation with human judgments.
(4)~Language-biased: works poorly for morphologically rich languages.
(5)~Insensitive to word order beyond short n-gram windows.
(6)~Reference-dependent: quality limited by reference count and quality.

Modern alternatives like COMET (neural, trained on human judgments) achieve
much higher correlation with human evaluation and should be preferred in
practice, but BLEU remains the lingua franca of MT reporting.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Cannot derive the formula—just says "it's n-gram overlap."
 
- Does not mention the brevity penalty or explain why it exists.
 
- Does not mention the clipping in modified precision.
 
- Claims BLEU measures recall (it measures precision).
 
- Cannot name any limitation.
questions.followups_source:
What is SacreBLEU and why was it created? How does BLEU compare to
ROUGE? What is COMET and why is it better? How would you evaluate MT for a
morphologically rich language like Finnish?

questions.question: Walk me through what happens, end to end, when a user types a query into a large-scale search engine.
questions.answer_source:
Structure the answer as the funnel, with candidate counts and latency at each stage.

**(1) Query understanding** ($\sim$5–10\,ms): normalize (Unicode, case, punctuation), spell-correct (noisy channel over a query-log LM, with correct-vs-suggest thresholds), segment and tag ("`nike red running shoes"` $\to$ brand/color/product slots), link entities to the catalog/KG, classify intent (navigational/informational/transactional; category vs.\ brand in commerce), and expand/rewrite (mined synonyms as discounted optional clauses; cached or distilled LLM rewrites).

**(2) Candidate retrieval** ($\sim$20–50\,ms, sources in parallel): lexical retrieval from an inverted index (BM25-family scoring, structured filters from the tags), dense retrieval via ANN over embeddings for semantic match, possibly structured/KG lookups. Union, dedupe, filter: $10^3$–$10^4$ candidates from a corpus of $10^7$–$10^9$. Retrieval is recall-oriented and decomposable; this stage bounds everything after it (the recall ceiling).

**(3) Ranking cascade**: L1 scores thousands with cheap features (BM25 fields, popularity, freshness, engagement priors) down to hundreds; L2 ($\sim$10–30\,ms) applies the real learned ranker—LambdaMART-style LTR or a cross-encoder—down to tens; L3 blends: personalization (capped, intent never overridden), business rules, diversity, compliance.

**(4) Presentation and logging**: snippets, facets, maybe an LLM answer; every impression and click is logged, becoming training data and judgments—search is a closed loop, and the biases of that loop (position bias, feedback loops) are why measurement is a first-class subsystem.

Close with segment awareness: head queries are cached and curated, torso queries are where ML has data, tail queries (the majority of distinct queries) lean on QU and semantic retrieval.
questions.red_flags_source:
- Starting at ranking—skipping query understanding entirely is the most common miss and instantly reads as "has never worked on search."
 
- No numbers: candidate counts and latency budgets are what make it an engineering answer rather than a diagram recitation.
 
- Describing one uniform pipeline with no head/torso/tail differentiation.
 
- No mention of the feedback loop from logging back to training.
questions.followups_source: "Where would this design change for an internal docs corpus of 10M documents?" "What breaks first when traffic grows 10$\times$?" "Which stages would you build first for a v1?"
questions.say:
I'd walk it as a funnel, with candidate counts and a latency budget at every stage.

Query understanding first, five to ten milliseconds, and skipping it is the fastest way to signal you've never worked on search. Normalize, spell-correct with a noisy-channel model over query logs, segment and tag — "nike red running shoes" becomes brand, color, product type — link entities to the catalog, classify intent, and expand with mined synonyms added as discounted optional clauses rather than hard terms.

Then candidate retrieval, twenty to fifty milliseconds, sources in parallel: an inverted index with BM25-family scoring plus the structured filters that fell out of tagging, and dense retrieval by ANN over embeddings for semantic match. Union, dedupe, filter, and you're at a thousand to ten thousand candidates out of ten million to a billion. This stage sets the recall ceiling for everything after it.

Then the ranking cascade. L1 scores thousands with cheap features — field BM25, popularity, freshness, engagement priors — down to hundreds. L2 is the real learned ranker, LambdaMART or a cross-encoder, ten to thirty milliseconds, down to tens. L3 blends personalization, capped so it never overrides expressed intent, plus business rules, diversity and compliance.

Then presentation and logging, and I'd close there deliberately, because search is a closed loop: every impression and click becomes training data, which is why position bias makes measurement a first-class subsystem. And head queries are cached and curated, torso is where ML has data, the tail leans on query understanding and semantic retrieval.
numbers: Query understanding ~5–10 ms, retrieval ~20–50 ms, L2 ranking ~10–30 ms
10⁷–10⁹ corpus → 10³–10⁴ candidates → hundreds → tens
red_flags: Starting at ranking and skipping query understanding entirely — the most common miss.
No numbers: without candidate counts and latency budgets it's a diagram recitation, not engineering.
One uniform pipeline with no head/torso/tail differentiation.
No mention of the logging loop feeding back into training.
followups: How does this change for an internal docs corpus of 10M documents?
What breaks first when traffic grows 10x?
Which stages would you build first for a v1?

questions.question: Your new L2 reranker improves offline NDCG by 4%, but online conversions are flat. Walk me through your diagnosis.
questions.answer_source:
Diagnose the funnel stage by stage, starting above the reranker.

**(1) The recall ceiling first.** The reranker reorders whatever retrieval hands it; if the candidate sets lack the genuinely good documents, a better ordering of mediocre candidates moves nothing. Judged-only offline eval hides this—the judged pool was built from what past systems retrieved. Check recall per stage against judged-relevant documents; if retrieval recall is the binding constraint, the fix is upstream of the model you just shipped.

**(2) Offline label contamination.** If the offline labels derive from clicks, they inherit the old ranker's position bias—"improvement" partly measures agreement with the incumbent plus noise (Chapter~). Re-evaluate on the bias-resistant anchors: editorial judgments and any randomized-traffic slice.

**(3) Where are the gains?** Slice the offline delta by segment and by position: gains concentrated on torso/tail queries that are a small share of traffic, or at positions below the fold, are real but commercially invisible. Traffic-weight the offline gain before expecting an online echo.

**(4) What actually got served?** L3 blending—business rules, merchandising, diversity—may be clobbering the new order. Measure the override rate: how often does the served order differ from the ranker's order, and did it change?

**(5) Presentation and metric distance.** A reordering with identical titles/images/prices may not change click behavior; and conversion is far downstream—check the intermediate chain (CTR@k, add-to-cart, reformulation rate) for movement. Finally, check power: the experiment may simply be underpowered for a conversion-sized effect (Chapter~).
questions.red_flags_source:
- "The offline metric must be wrong" or "ship it anyway"—no decomposition, no diagnosis.
 
- Not reaching for per-stage recall—the recall-ceiling check is the expected first move.
 
- Never mentioning click-label position bias when the offline labels are behavioral.
questions.followups_source: "How do you maintain a randomized slice cheaply and ethically?" "The gains were all on tail queries—what would make them show up in conversions?" "Offline says worse, online says better—now what?"

Measure per-stage recall against judged-relevant documents; if retrieval is binding, the fix is upstream of what you shipped.

Then question the offline number. If those labels came from clicks they carry the old ranker's position bias, so part of your four percent is measuring agreement with the incumbent. Re-run against editorial judgments or a randomized-traffic slice, which don't have that circularity.

Look at CTR and add-to-cart for movement, and confirm the test could detect a conversion-sized effect.
